When the time arrives, they shall have the lay attendants and śrāmaṇeras strike the *ghanṭī* three times. All bhikṣus within the boundary shall assemble, with the sole exception of those who have not yet...
Those who have received the precepts but have committed an offense and have not yet confessed it are not permitted to listen [to the recitation].

However, if there is a cause such as illness, or for matters concerning the Sangha that are in accordance with the Dharma, they are permitted to grant their consent (*chanda*). If the matter is trivial or not a legitimate matter of the Sangha, they are not permitted to grant consent.

As for those present in the assembly, if there are individuals who deserve censure, they must not be censured; this is called the "assembling of the Sangha. From within this harmonious Sangha, one person is appointed.

The presiding *karmadāna* shall perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) and the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). The reciter shall sit upon a high seat, while the listeners sit on lower seats.
Each person shall don their seven-strip robe (*saptaka-cīvara*) and sit in order. If there are no obstacles or impediments, the entire text of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* should be recited in full.

If there are obstacles or impediments, the recitation shall cease at the point reached. For the remainder, one says: "The Sangha has heard it regularly. Or, if there is an urgent matter and the time for recitation cannot be observed, [the procedure is as follows].

One should immediately rise from one's seat. If there are persons of influence who insist on coming to hear the precepts, one may recite them the day before, or extend the recitation until the following day.
Or, if someone arrives while the recitation is in progress, one should simply stop and say, "The Sangha hears this constantly.
If there are those who insistently demand that the recitation be finished, one should recite by scrambling the phrasing and punctuation, so that they cannot understand it.
When the bhikṣu reciting the precepts makes an error, the bhikṣu seated next to him should provide the correct wording.
If there is some circumstance that prevents him from completing the recitation, the bhikṣu seated next to him should recite it in his stead.
If, on the day of reciting the precepts, there is no bhikṣu capable of reciting them, one should instead recite the verses of the brief instructions of the seven Buddhas.
If that is also not possible, one should recite: "Do no evil; practice all good; purify your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas."
The Buddha ordained that a bhikṣu of five years' standing must recite the Prātimokṣa. If he does not recite it, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If he is unable to do so, he shall never be permitted to live apart from his teacher for the rest of his life.

If there is one bhikṣu residing [there], on the day of the *poṣadha*, he should go to the *poṣadha* hall, sprinkle and sweep it until it is clean, spread out the seating mats, prepare the water pitcher for rinsing, light the lamps, and arrange the voting sticks (*śalākā*).
If visiting bhikṣus arrive—whether four or more than four—he should first inform them, and then perform the *poṣadha*. Facing one another, they should say: "Today, the Sangha’s fifteenth [day]..."
The recitation of the precepts: "I (so-and-so) am pure. Thus it is said three times. If there is only one person, they should mentally reflect and speak these words aloud;
thus it is said three times. If there are three persons, they may not receive the declaration of desire for purity from a fourth person.
If there are two persons, they may not receive the declaration of desire for purity from a third person. If there is one person, they may not receive the declaration of desire from a second person.
[The assembly] is pure. Each person should speak for themselves.
On the day of the *poṣadha*, if visiting *bhikṣus* arrive and the visiting *bhikṣus* are few, they should seek harmony with the resident *bhikṣus* to recite the precepts together.
If the visiting *bhikṣus* who have arrived are equal in number to the resident *bhikṣus*, they should likewise seek [harmony] from the resident *bhikṣus*.

The formal assembly shall recite the *Poṣadha* together. If the resident bhikṣus are few and the visiting bhikṣus are many, one should seek the formal assembly from the visiting bhikṣus to recite the *Poṣadha* together.

If, on the day of the *Poṣadha*, the resident bhikṣus have gathered and are about to recite the introduction to the *Poṣadha-sūtra*, and there arrive visiting bhikṣus who are few in number, [one should...]

One should announce the purity (*pārisuddhi*). Those seated in order should listen. If the recitation has already concluded and the assembly has completely dispersed, one must likewise announce the purity.

Should one fail to do so, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma. If visiting monks arrive who are equal in number to the resident monks, or if they are more numerous than the resident monks, the precepts should be recited anew for them.
Should they not do so, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma. If the resident monks are reciting the precepts and resident monks arrive...

Whether they are fewer, equal, or more, it is as previously described. If visiting bhikṣus recite the precepts and resident bhikṣus arrive, whether they are fewer, equal, or more, it is also as previously described.
Bodhisattva bhikṣus shall perform the poṣadha separately. Those who have not yet received the bodhisattva precepts are not permitted to listen.

Likewise, those who have violated the precepts and have not yet attained purity are not permitted to listen. Every half-month, before images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they shall recite the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts.
If there is only one person, that single person shall recite them; if there are two, three, or even up to a hundred, they shall do so together.
A thousand [people] shall likewise recite it, one person at a time. The reciter shall sit on a high seat, while the listeners sit on lower seats.

Each shall don their nine-strip, seven-strip, or five-strip *kāṣāya* robe and sit in order. Should anyone have committed an offense, they must come forth from the assembly and confess their transgression.
Those who have violated the ten heavy precepts should perform repentance, reciting the ten heavy and forty-eight light precepts with utmost sincerity throughout the six periods of the day and night.
One should pay homage to the Buddhas of the three periods of time; if one beholds auspicious signs—whether light or flowers—one’s transgressions will be extinguished.
Those who have committed minor offenses (*āpatti*) should confess and repent face-to-face with another; their transgressions will then be extinguished.
Bodhisattva bhikṣus should likewise listen to the exposition of the bhikṣu precepts; those who do not listen incur an offense against the Dharma (*vaidharmya-āpatti*).

Since the *saṃvara-śīla* (precepts of restraint) encompasses everything without exception, and since the Buddha established the monastic regulations within the Saṅgha based upon the Śrāvaka dharma, once they have resided together, they must listen together.
However, there are differences regarding what is permitted or prohibited therein, and the degrees of gravity vary accordingly.
This is because their practices and vows differ. Regarding those who wish to speak, on the day of the *poṣadha* ceremony,
if there are matters concerning the Saṃgha that accord with the Dharma, or if there are reasons such as illness, they may do so.
If one wishes to come but is unable to do so, they shall convey their intention of consent (*chanda*) to another person to communicate on their behalf.
This person should maintain proper deportment and go to the individual to whom the consent is to be transmitted, speaking as follows: "Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind.

I, [Name], a bhikṣu, grant my consent and purity regarding the legal matters of the Saṃgha. That person who conveys the consent shall then go before the Saṃgha, where the members of the Saṃgha will inquire.

If there are those who wish to express their *yukta-viśuddhi* (consent and purity), they should immediately emerge from the assembly, adjust their deportment, and say: "Venerable sirs, please attend to me with one mind.
Now, the bhikṣu [Name] has granted his consent and purity for the formal act of the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma. Having said this once, he should cease.
Alternatively, if there is a sick person who cannot come and there is no one to convey the consent, the Saṃgha should dispatch someone to go and receive the consent from the sick person. Sick...

A person should say: "I, [Name], because of the cause of illness, give my consent for purity (*chanda-śuddhi*). The one who receives the consent shall return to the Saṃgha and speak in this same manner."

When a person who has received the *chanda* (consent) has already received it, if there is some external circumstance preventing them from going to the Saṃgha to express it, they should be granted the *chanda* again.

Alternatively, if the person who received the *chanda* has already arrived at the Saṃgha, but then falls asleep, enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*), or forgets to act intentionally, the granting of the *chanda* is still valid.
If, however, one intentionally fails to speak [the consent], one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
A person who has received the *yadṛcchā* (consent/vote) from one individual may also receive the *yadṛcchā* from another. Upon arriving in the midst of the Saṃgha, they should announce:
"So-and-so and so-and-so [grant] their *yadṛcchā* for the formal act of the Saṃgha (*dharmika saṃghakarma*) and their purity (*pariśuddhi*).

Alternatively, if there are many people and it is not possible to announce each name individually, one should simply announce: "Now there are many bhikṣus who grant their *yadṛcchā* for the formal act of the Saṃgha and their purity."
If there is a sick bhikṣu who is unable to give his consent (*chanda*), he should be carried into the midst of the Saṃgha.
If he cannot be moved, the great assembly should go to the sick person's location and recite the precepts for him.
If there is a bhikṣu who has given his consent for a matter and then ceases activity once that matter is concluded, he may go and listen to the recitation of the precepts.
If he does not go to listen, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

If it is the time for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) within the Saṃgha, one should say: "I grant my consent (*chanda*) for the *pravāraṇā*. The remaining phrasing is identical [to the other formal acts].

Whenever a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is being performed within the Saṃgha, those who are unable to attend the assembly must all grant their consent; however, this excludes the delimitation of boundaries (*sīmābandhana*), for at that time everyone must assemble in person.

Regarding the *vassa* (rainy season retreat): The Buddha first established the three-month summer *vassa* originally for the purpose of protecting living beings, because within even a square foot of ground during the summer months, there are invariably insects;
thus it was so ordained. It begins on the sixteenth day of the fourth month and concludes on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
One should address the person upon whom one relies, saying: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], am now entering the three-month summer retreat;
because this dwelling is dilapidated, I shall repair it. This is to be said three times. That person replies: "I know; do not be negligent. One answers: "So be it."
Recite this. If there is no person upon whom one can rely, one should mentally resolve: "I, [Name], shall observe the three-month rains retreat in reliance upon such-and-such monastery.
For those observing the later retreat, change the word "former" to "later"; the rest is the same.

Even if one arrives at the place of residence for the retreat but forgets to formally conclude it, the retreat is still valid. Furthermore, the moment one arrives at that place, the retreat is established.
The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states: One may observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in a location free from five faults: first, being too far from a village, making it difficult to obtain alms;
second, being too close to a city, which hinders the path of practice; and third, being a place with many mosquitoes and ants, which causes harm to both oneself and others.
Fourth, there is no one who may be relied upon unless they possess five virtues. Fifth, there is no donor to provide food, drink, clothing, or medicine. Those who possess these five virtues are:
first, those who cause others to hear what they have not heard; second, those who cause what has already been heard to become pure; third, those who are able to provide resolution.
4. It enables one to penetrate [the teachings] without obstruction. 5. It eliminates false views and brings about right view.
Regarding the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), it is not necessarily required to stay entirely within a monastery.

One may instead stay in an *āraṇya* (forest hermitage), at the foot of a tree, in the fork of a tree, in a stone cave, in a pointed-roof hut, or on a boat—provided that the head is not obstructed when sitting and there is enough space for the knees. All of these are permissible.
One may enter the rains retreat (*varṣā*), provided one avoids the first five faults. For a bhikṣuṇī to enter the rains retreat without observing these is a *pāyattika* offense;

for the other four assemblies to do so is a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding those who come to enter the retreat: those who arrive on the sixteenth day of the fourth month are said to be entering the "early retreat" (*pūrvavarṣā*);
those who arrive on the seventeenth day or the fifteenth day of the fifth month are said to be entering the "late retreat" (*paścimavarṣā*). This refers to the early retreat.

One should reside during the first three-month period and the subsequent period of settled residence for the latter three months; both must complete exactly ninety days. If they are not completed, one does not attain the *varṣa* (the annual retreat).
Those who observe the first retreat perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; those who observe the later retreat likewise perform the *pravāraṇā*.

After those who observed the first retreat have performed their *pravāraṇā*, they count the *varṣa*; however, this is not permitted for those who observed the later retreat, because the ninety days have not been fulfilled. The first...
When those who have completed the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) divide the goods they have acquired, those who entered the retreat later should also be allotted a share.

They should be made to remain until the days are completed [to fulfill the full term]. Furthermore, some say there are three types of *varṣā*: entering before the sixteenth day of the fourth month is the "early retreat" (*pūrvavarṣā*); from the seventeenth day to the fifteenth day of the fifth month is the "middle retreat" (*madhyamavarṣā*); and on the sixteenth day is the "late retreat" (*paścimavarṣā*). All these complete the count of ninety days for the year.
Once the *varṣā* has concluded, if there is a legitimate matter or occasion requiring one to go elsewhere, one must return on that very same day. If one is unable to do so...
Regarding those who return on that very day: they are permitted to receive the seven-day rule (*saptāha-vidhi*), provided they shall return within seven days.

To receive this rule, one simply declares before another person as follows: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], receive the seven-day rule for the sake of [a certain] matter, so that I may return here to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*).
This is stated once. If, due to circumstances, one is unable to return within seven days, it is permitted to receive the rule for exceeding seven days.
Whether for fifteen days or one month, one should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one subsequent proclamation), saying: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let [so-and-so] receive the *saptāha-atireka-vidhi* (the rule for exceeding seven days)—whether for fifteen days or one month—for the sake of a certain matter, so as to return here to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*). The motion is thus. The text of the *karman* may be recited accordingly.
[One] should know that (if there are several people who may perform the *karmavācanā* together).

If a bhikṣu, having completed the rains retreat (*varṣā*), receives the seven-day permission (*saptāha-kalpa*) and goes outside the boundary, returning after the seven days have passed, that bhikṣu breaks his previous rains retreat;
because he has violated his original commitment, he incurs an offense. If a bhikṣu, at the end of the rains retreat, subsequently receives the seven-day...

Regarding the *saptāha-vidhi* (seven-day rule): if a monk goes outside the boundary and returns, or does not return, he does not violate his previous *pūrvavarṣā* (early rains retreat) and does not contravene his original commitment;
therefore, there is no offense.
If a monk accepts the seven-day rule and goes outside the boundary, but is detained by his mother and returns after the seven days have passed, he does not lose [the validity of the retreat].

Regarding the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat): if a bhikṣu, having received the seven-day authorization (*saptāha-vidhi*), goes outside the boundary, and due to impassable water or land, danger from bandits, danger from wild beasts, or similar obstacles, returns after more than seven days, he does not lose his *varṣā*.
If a bhikṣu has entered the rains retreat and perceives within it obstacles to pure conduct or threats to life, he should go and inform the donor and request to move elsewhere.
If the donor consents, that is well; if they do not consent, he may depart for those reasons without violating the rains retreat.
If a bhikṣu has completed the rains retreat and is unable to obtain food, drink, robes, or medicine, he may depart on account of this matter.
Or, if the location is infested with many venomous insects and he fears harming living beings, he may depart on account of this matter.
Or, if there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who intend to employ means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, he may depart on account of this matter; yet he does not break his rains retreat.
If there is a bhikṣu staying alone during the retreat (varṣā), and he intends to receive the seven-day authorization (saptāha-karman), he should mentally reflect and speak these words:

"I, the bhikṣu [Name], now receive the seven-day authorization; having passed the seven days, etc., I shall go outside the boundary for the sake of [a certain] matter, and return here to this very place to continue the retreat" (recite this three times).

Regarding *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence): it means allowing others to freely point out one’s faults. Having cultivated the path for ninety days and refined both body and mind, many people become deluded regarding themselves and fail to reflect upon their own transgressions.
Now, by voluntarily proclaiming one’s own offenses, one permits the Saṃgha to point out those faults; hence it is called *pravāraṇā*.
When the ninety-day period of the rains retreat is complete, the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) is held on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight.
If a bhikṣuṇī arrives, the bhikṣus perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fourteenth day, while the bhikṣuṇīs perform theirs on the fifteenth.

On that day, whether during the morning meal or the midday meal, one should go to the hall for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha-śālā*), strike the *ghanṭā* to assemble the community, and ensure that those who have not received full ordination (*upasampadā*) do not join. The officiant should then announce: "Great..."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Today, on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, the community of monks has assembled at [place name] for the *pravāraṇā*.

Once the Saṃgha has assembled, two persons qualified to receive the *pravāraṇā* should first be appointed. These two individuals must each possess five qualities. First, the five qualities of one who performs the *pravāraṇā*:

they are free from attachment, free from hatred, free from fear, free from delusion, and they know whether the *pravāraṇā* has been performed or not yet performed. Second, the five qualities of one who raises a charge: they know the proper time.
Not at an improper time; according to reality; not with falsehood; that which is beneficial, not that which is unbeneficial;
gently, not harshly; with a mind of loving-kindness, not with anger. If the assembly is large, two persons are appointed together; if the assembly is small...
Appoint one person to perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. The formal announcement (*jñapti*) is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu [Name] as the recipient of the *pravāraṇā*. This is the announcement. The text for the *karman* may be understood accordingly.
Once the *karman* has been performed, the two recipients of the *pravāraṇā* shall then rise from their seats and go before the senior monk (*sthavira*) to pay homage.
This is sufficient. The formal motion (*jñapti*) is as follows: "Venerable Sangha, listen. Today the community of monks performs the *pravāraṇā*.

If the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha permits, may the Sangha, being in harmony, perform the *pravāraṇā*. This is the motion. The two individuals should each bare their right shoulders, remove their leather sandals, kneel with their right knees on the ground, and join their palms.
They should perform the *pravāraṇā* starting from the senior monk (*sthavira*), saying: "Venerable community of monks, today is the day of *pravāraṇā*."
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], also perform the *pravāraṇā*. If there be any offense seen, heard, or suspected, may the Venerable Elders, out of compassion, speak to me.
If I see the offense, I shall deal with it according to the Dharma. (Recite this three times. The Saṃgha should then rise from their seats in succession.
When the *pravāraṇā* is finished, two persons should go before the Elder and announce: "The Saṃgha has unanimously completed the *pravāraṇā*."
They should withdraw as they usually do after performing the prostrations. If there are those who are elderly or ill, they may speak before the two [elders] while remaining in their original seats.

Alternatively, on the day of the *pravāraṇā*, if eight kinds of calamities arise and one is unable to speak at length, one should speak briefly—either twice, once, or each person together three times.
If the calamities are so urgent that one cannot speak together three times, then immediately...
One should depart from this difficult situation.

Alternatively, if there are four or fewer persons, they should perform the *pratimukha* (face-to-face) method; they must all assemble together and perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) among one another.
Each person should say: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. Today is the day of the *pravāraṇā* for the Saṃgha. I, [Name], a bhikṣu, am pure. This is to be said three times. If...
If there are three people, or even two, they should follow this same rule.
If there is only one person at the residence, on the day of the *pravāraṇā*, he should go to the hall for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), sweep it, and spread out the seating mats.
When waiting for visiting bhikṣus, if there are no visiting bhikṣus, one should mentally reflect and speak these words aloud: "Today the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am pure. This is to be recited three times.

After the *pravāraṇā*, one should undergo the *varṣa* (the annual reckoning of seniority). Regarding this *varṣa*: those who have left the household life do not calculate their years by their birth year;
rather, they must take the completion of a summer retreat (*vassa*) as one year. Those who have committed offenses or who have broken the rules of the retreat do not receive the seniority.
This begins from the sixteenth day of the seventh month. Furthermore, it is said that "lunar" (*la*) signifies the meaning of "junction," referring to when—
The sixteenth day of the seventh month marks the New Year, the occasion for the transition between the old year and the new.

According to the words of the Buddha regarding medicinal substances, there are four types: first, medicine taken at the proper time (*kālabhaiṣajya*); second, medicine not restricted to the proper time (*akālabhaiṣajya*); third, seven-day medicine (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*); and fourth, lifetime medicine (*yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*).
Medicine for longevity. Regarding "timely food" (*kālabhojana*), there are two kinds: first, *pūjaniya* food, which refers to rice, parched grain flour, dry cakes, and so forth;
second, *khādaniya* food, which refers to stalks, leaves, flowers, fruits, and fine powders.
These two types of food may be eaten from the appearance of dawn until midday; this is called "timely food. One who receives such food must first discern and recognize it.

Regarding what constitutes food and what does not: there must be two factors—the donor's intention to give—and three factors—the gift must be bestowed in accordance with the Dharma—for one to be permitted to receive the food.

As for "medicines taken outside of the proper time": once the sun has passed its zenith, the first two types of food may no longer be consumed. However, there may be occasions due to illness or other causes where this restriction does not apply.

The Buddha permitted the making of syrups from the juices of pears, jujubes, *mṛdvīkā* grapes, sugarcane, and so forth. If they do not cause intoxication, they may be drunk outside of the prescribed time (*akāla*).

Furthermore, one must not receive syrup on one day and keep it until the next; if one drinks it [after such storage], one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* further permits honey-syrup.

If various syrups are as clear as the color of water, and have been purified by dropping water [into them], one may receive them from the hands of a pure person and consume them in comparison [with the rules].
The Master adds the ritual for receiving the dharma, saying: "Virtuous One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], now because of the cause and condition of thirst, have this [Name] of a drink. Desiring to consume it outside of the proper time, I now receive it from you, Virtuous One. This is recited three times.
If one drinks when not suffering from thirst, one incurs an offense.
Regarding the seven-day medicines, the Buddha said: "There are five kinds: ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar.

Due to the causal condition of illness, I permit their consumption outside of the proper time. The procedure for formal acceptance is as follows: 'Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], now because of the causal condition of [specific] illness, have these seven-day medicines—such as ghee—in order to keep them overnight and consume them for seven days. I now [offer them] to the Venerable sir...'"
[This is] a boundary-reception. It is recited three times. If one keeps [these medicines] for more than seven days, one incurs an offense.
Regarding medicines for life: these include all salty, bitter, sour, and pungent substances that are unfit for food, such as ginger, pepper, and various types of pills and powders.
The Buddha permitted their lifelong use. To perform the formal reception, one says: "Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind. I..."
"Venerable [Name], due to the cause of illness, these [items] are medicines for as long as life lasts.
Because I wish to keep them overnight and consume them over a long period, I now receive them from you, Venerable Sir. (Recite this three times.)

Regarding the distribution of the property of a deceased monk among the five assemblies: if a member of the sangha passes away, none of his clothing or personal effects may be claimed by others; they belong exclusively to the Sangha.

This is because the requisites of one who has left the household life must necessarily be obtained from the Sangha, and since there is no portion for the Buddha or the Dharma, such items must enter the Sangha. However, the Sangha consists of both the four quarters [of the world] and those currently present.
Regarding the distinctions between things, there is a differentiation between light and heavy. The method for classifying these items is detailed as follows:
First, examining debts and obligations. The Buddha said: One should ask the caregiver, "Who owes goods to the patient? To whom does the patient owe goods?
If someone owes goods to the patient, one should collect them on their behalf and place them in the Sangha. If the patient owes goods to others, one should hold onto [the items] for a long time.
One should compensate him with robes; if there are none, one should sell one's three robes to compensate him. If there is a surplus, it should be given to the attendant.
Second, regarding the inquiry for instructions: the Buddha said that one should ask the attendant, "Does the patient have any instructions? If he says:
When a patient is at the point of death, they may say: "Give these things to the Buddha, to the Dharma, to the Saṃgha, to a stūpa, or to a person.
If [the items] are given after [the patient] has passed away, the Buddha said: "They should be requested back and distributed among the present Saṃgha. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If something was given to a person while alive but has not yet been taken away, the Saṃgha should grant it to them through a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*)."

Third, regarding the relinquishing of items: the *Saṃghāṭī* states that if a sick person dies, one should take the door-bolt and hand it over to the monastery’s administrative officer (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*), and only then perform the offering of the relics.
The *Vinayamātṛkā* says: "After first enshrouding and burying the deceased, the funeral procession departs.
Once the monks have returned to the monastery, they place the deceased monk’s robes and belongings before the assembly. The one who has brought them forth says: 'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"
"A certain bhikṣu has passed away while residing at this monastery. All his robes and personal effects shall be distributed among the monks present at this monastery.
Thus he relinquishes them, saying this three times.
Regarding the four categories of light and heavy items: the Buddha said, "If a member of the fivefold assembly dies, all that they possess shall belong entirely to the Saṃgha.
This includes fields and gardens, fruit trees, separate rooms, and items belonging to those separate rooms;

copper jars, copper basins, axes and chisels, lamp stands, rope beds, sitting mats, bedding, woolen rugs, carriages, and the water pitchers, washing basins, and utensils belonging to the monastery attendant."
The staff of tin, iron utensils, wooden utensils, earthenware, leather utensils, bamboo utensils, and various other heavy items should not be divided;

they belong to the Saṃgha of the Four Directions. As for light items such as razors, robes, bowls, sitting mats, needle cases, and *kūñcika* (keys) or similar vessels, these may be divided by the present Saṃgha.
Among the assembly, one person should be appointed to distribute those items that are to be shared.
Regarding indivisible items, [the Buddha said that] they should each be placed in a separate location and given to the five types of attendants.
The Buddha said: "An attendant must possess five qualities. One who has accomplished these five qualities should be given the patient's clothing and requisites.
What are the five qualities? First, knowing what the patient may eat and what they may not eat; if it is permissible to eat, one should provide it."
1. One does not loathe the excrement, urine, saliva, or vomit of the sick. 2. One possesses a heart of compassion and does not act for the sake of food or clothing.

3. One is able to manage the medicinal decoctions until the patient recovers or dies. 4. One is able to preach the Dharma for the sake of the sick person, thereby increasing one’s own merit in wholesome dharmas.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are four types of temporary service: that which is appointed by the Saṃgha, or that which is undertaken of one’s own accord.
If performed for the sake of pleasure or for the sake of a wrong livelihood, it does not merit a reward.

However, if one nurses a patient for their benefit, desiring that they recover quickly—even down to lighting a single lamp wick—and the patient should pass away during that time, this also merits a reward. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"When many people nurse a patient, the reward should be given to the one who attended until the end. The *Mātṛkā* states: "Even a layperson who nurses a patient should be given a small amount [of reward]. Thus said the Buddha.
It is said: "The attendant of the sick person should be granted six items: a needle case, a garment container, and a storage vessel.
These should be granted by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation). The motion is as follows: 'Venerable Saṃgha, listen! The bhikṣu [Name] has passed away.

All his three robes and other belongings should be divided among the Saṃgha present here. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant permission. The Saṃgha now grants [these items] to the attendant bhikṣu [Name].'"
The Venerable Kāśyapa said: "It is thus. The *karmavācanā* text may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the distribution of light items among six portions: when five or more persons are living together and one person dies, a successive distribution (*parivartaka-bhāga*) must be made.
The Saṃgha shall appoint one person by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. The announcement (*jñapti*) is as follows: "May the venerable Saṃgha listen. The bhikṣu [Name] has passed away."

All clothing and items present should be divided among the Saṃgha. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, we now take these clothing and items and give them to the bhikṣu (so-and-so, so-and-so), with the understanding that they shall be returned to the Saṃgha.
The motion is thus; the *karmavācanā* text may be understood accordingly.
Having performed this rite, one should take as many robes and articles as are present and divide them according to the number [of monks]. Guest monks who arrive shall also receive a share;
however, those who arrive only after the distribution of the robes has already been completed do not receive a share. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If it is not distributed universally..."

The Sangha shall give one [robe] to a monk who possesses no robes at all. If a single robe is of excellent quality and there is no need to cut it down, and if such robes are available for all, they should be distributed according to seniority;
however, if a specific one is required, it should be given directly to that person.
When four people live together and one dies, they should divide the rewards for the nurse equally.

Only the three remaining members should act in harmony and hand over the robes, saying: "Venerable sirs, please take note: we now offer the robes, bowl, and other belongings of the deceased bhikṣu [Name]."
[This is] said three times to the bhikṣu who is tending to the sick. For all other light items, a formal motion with a subsequent announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) is made as follows:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. The bhikṣu [Name] has passed away; all his robes and requisites should be divided by the Saṃgha present here.
This is the motion. The text for the formal act (karman) is to be understood accordingly. When visiting bhikṣus arrive, it is the same as before.
Three people were living together. When one of them died, the reward for nursing the patient should be divided among them.

The two remaining persons should reach an agreement and hand over their robes as described above. As for the other light articles, they should divide them by speaking three times to one another, saying: "Venerable sirs, listen."
"These robes and personal effects of the deceased bhikṣu [Name] should belong to us. This is to be recited three times. When visiting bhikṣus arrive, it is the same as before.
If two persons live together and one dies, the survivor takes the robe with his hand and says: "These robes and personal effects of the deceased bhikṣu [Name] should belong to me.
This is to be recited three times. As for the visiting bhikṣus who have arrived, they must not take hold of the robe with their hands.

If there are items sought for a sick person—such as medicine, clothing, or food—or for the sake of stūpa affairs or monastic affairs, even if they are not present, one portion should be given [to the deceased].

If there is a *karmadāna* (lay attendant), he shall also receive half a portion. If the deceased dies in the home of a layperson (*avadātavasana*), light articles shall be divided among the five groups of monks present;
heavy articles shall be sent to a nearby monastery (*saṃghārāma*). If no five groups of monks are present, they shall be sent together [to such a place].
With the local saṃghārāma;
the six classes of penance for confessing the pārajika offenses.
*Pārājika*. This is translated as "abandonment," meaning that one is permanently cast out from the ocean-like boundary of the Buddha’s teaching, having no further share in the fruits of the Path.

One who commits this offense should be expelled. However, if after committing it, one has no intention of concealment and earnestly seeks repentance, one should grant them the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the ritual for those granted training).
To one granted these precepts, thirty-five matters are revoked; they must practice these for the remainder of their life and may not transcend them.

If he departs, or if the Saṃgha is performing the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) or a formal act (*karmavācanā*), there is no offense whether he comes or does not come. If he commits another grave offense, he should be expelled (*pravāsanīya*).
Only when he is able to realize the fruit of Arhatship does he transcend [the stage of a novice] and enter the rank of the Great Saṃgha.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "This constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*). Even while weeping, he refused to leave his *kāṣāya*. Furthermore, for one who deeply delights in the Buddha-dharma, one should grant him the training in the precepts (*śikṣamāṇā*).
Regarding the training in the precepts: if a bhikṣu’s food is impure, his [the trainee’s] food is also impure;
if his food is impure, the bhikṣu’s food is also impure. One may give him food that exceeds the limit, with the exception of the five types of living seeds that have been purified by fire."
Regarding gold and silver: having already accepted food from a śrāmaṇera, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"All those who receive and practice the precepts ordained by the Buddha must sit below the great bhikṣus.

They must not stay overnight in the same room as the great saṃgha for more than three nights. Furthermore, they themselves must not stay in the same room as those who have not yet received full ordination."

During the constellation of Śravaṇā (the Room), after two nights have passed, one may perform the two types of formal acts (*karmas*) for the Saṃgha: the invitation for self-reflection (*pravāraṇā*) and the confession (*poṣadha*).

However, one may not count toward the quorum for granting precepts or the expiation of offenses. As for other communal legal procedures, they may not be performed; yet, the calculation of the year (*varṣā*) may be received.
One must not recite the Vinaya within the assembly; however, it is permitted if no one else is present.
The *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharma for confession:

*saṃghāvaśeṣa* is translated here as "Saṃgha-remainder. This means the offense is adjacent to [the most serious category of] expulsion (*pārājika*). It is like a person who has been struck by another and barely retains their throat;
it is logically appropriate that they be rescued immediately. As for the offender: if they conceal [the offense], they should follow its [prescribed] duration.
If he conceals it, he is given *pārivāsika* (probation). When the *pārivāsika* period is completed, he is given six nights of *mānatva* (penance).
When the *mānatva* is completed, he is granted absolution (*ābṛhaṇa*) before an assembly of twenty monks.
If he has committed an offense but did not conceal it, he is directly assigned *mānatva*. When the six nights are completed, he is then granted absolution before an assembly of twenty monks. If...

Regarding those who repeatedly commit offenses among the two types of disciplinary practices (*dvividha-prāyaścitta*), they shall be granted the *mūlāpakarṣa* (root-punishment) and the *parivāsa*—the latter being translated as "separate dwelling.
This means that once the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been performed, thirty-five privileges are revoked.

One who has committed the eight offenses against a junior monk must forfeit the night; they must confess before the Saṃgha and provide service to the community for as many days as the offense was concealed.
*Mānatva* means "extremely painful and base conduct"; in general outline, it is similar to *parivāsa*.
However, staying overnight among the saṃgha is what makes it distinct.

Regarding the method for repenting a sthūlātyaya offense—sthūlātyaya being translated here as "ugly" or "vile"—there are two types: first, those arising from [other offenses]; second, independent ones. As for those arising from [other offenses]: sthūlātyaya...
There are three grades of *sthūlātyaya*. That which arises from a *pārājika* offense and is grave is called the superior grade; one must confess it before the entire Saṃgha.
If it arises from a *pārājika* offense and is light, or if it arises from a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and is grave, it is called the middle grade;
one must go outside the boundary and confess it before an assembly of four bhikṣus. If it arises from a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and is light, one should...
One should confess before a single pure bhikṣu. A *sthūlātyaya* committed independently also has three grades.

Those of the highest grade include, for example, causing a schism in the Saṃgha regarding the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, killing a deva, or stealing four *kārsāpaṇas* or more; these are called the highest grade.

Those such as causing a schism in the Saṃgha regarding formal procedures (*karmavācanā*), stealing three *kārsāpaṇas*, or two *kārsāpaṇas* are called the middle grade. Those such as eating raw flesh or blood, or reviling with an evil mind [are the lowest grade].
If a monk steals one *māṣaka* or more, it is classified as the lower grade of offense; the repentance for all three grades is identical to that prescribed by the *Prātimokṣa*.

Regarding the method for confessing a *pāyattika* offense, this category is divided into two parts: the first is called *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, which is translated here as "forfeiture and expiation. Its procedure is as follows:
All of these involve transgressions regarding material objects. Because one is now penalized by having those objects forfeited to the Saṃgha, they are called *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Another name is *pāyattika*, which means "falling"; since these offenses pertain solely to conduct and speech without any physical object to be forfeited, they are simply termed "falling."

Regarding the confession and relinquishment of an *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense: this object must not be relinquished apart from the community (*saṃgha*). If it is relinquished otherwise, the relinquishment is invalid and one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One should go before the *saṃgha*, bare the right shoulder, remove one’s leather sandals, prostrate at the feet of the senior monks, then kneel on the right knee with palms joined, and say:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], intentionally possessed [such-and-such] items..."

Extravagant robes: an offense involving forfeiture and expiation (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). I now relinquish them to the Saṃgha. Having thus declared the relinquishment of the robes once, one immediately requests confession within the Saṃgha, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], intentionally kept [number] extravagant robes, thereby committing an offense involving forfeiture and expiation.
These robes have already been relinquished to the Saṃgha; now there are numerous *pāyattika* offenses arising from..."
The *saṃgha* requests confession: "May the *saṃgha* grant me, the bhikṣu [Name], the opportunity for confession out of compassion.

After this has been recited three times, one should request the presiding master of confession. This presiding master must be one who has not committed an offense, or one who, having committed one, has already completed the confession;
such a person is called a pure bhikṣu and is fit to receive the confession. Arranging one’s deportment, one should say: "Venerable Sir..."
With single-minded attention, [the offender] says: "I, the bhikṣu [Name], now request the Venerable One to act as the presiding master for the confession of a *pāyattika* offense.
May the Venerable One act as my presiding master for the confession of this *pāyattika* offense, out of compassion.

This should be recited three times. The person receiving the confession must not answer immediately; rather, they should first make the following announcement: "May the Sangha of Venerable Ones listen. This [Name]..."

A) A bhikṣu intentionally keeps several extra robes beyond the permitted limit; he commits an offense of expiation with forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). He must forfeit these robes to the Saṃgha.
Within this matter, there are numerous *pāyattika* offenses, for which he is to be made to beg for forgiveness from the Saṃgha.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha grants its consent, I, [Name] Bhikṣu, shall accept the confession of [Name] Bhikṣu. Thus is the formal motion (*jñapti*). [The motion is] performed.

After this announcement has been made, one should then say to them: "So be it. The person confessing their offense, assuming the proper deportment, says: "Venerable Sir, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, [Name], have intentionally kept several extra robes in excess of the permitted limit, thereby committing an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
These robes have now been forfeited to the Saṃgha. As for the numerous *pāyattika* offenses incurred, I now openly confess and repent before the Venerable One; I dare not [conceal them]."
Concealment [of an offense] leads to suffering; confession brings peace and happiness. One who confesses an offense remembered and revealed does not remain scattered or concealed despite knowing it.
Having recited three times: "May the Venerable One bear in mind that I am pure, that my body of precepts is complete, and that my *poṣadha* is pure," the one receiving the confession should say:
"Reprove your own mind and give rise to weary detachment. The respondent should answer: "So be it."
After the confession has been performed, the robe should be returned. Within the Saṃgha, one should examine whether the property can be returned or not.
For example, if it was made into bedding from wild silkworm cotton, it cannot be returned; it must be cut into pieces, mixed with mud, and used to plaster walls or earthen mounds.

Regarding the five types of surplus items—extra robes, extra bowls, robes kept for more than one month, robes received as urgent gifts, and leftover medicine—one should immediately transfer them back to the assembly on that very seat.
As for other offenses, they should be directly returned on that very seat. Regarding "immediate transfer," the Buddha said:
if it is difficult for the Saṃgha to assemble, and this bhikṣu has a reason to travel far away, he should ask [the assembly] as follows:
"To whom shall the object be given? It should be given to whoever was mentioned. Once it has been given, one should return it to the Saṃgha by performing a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.

The formal announcement (*jñapti*) is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! The bhikṣu [Name] intentionally kept several extra robes and committed an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
This robe has already been forfeited to the Saṃgha. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, I shall now take this robe..."
[Give this] to bhikṣu [Name]. Bhikṣu [Name] shall return this to bhikṣu [Name]. The motion (*jñapti*) is as follows: "May the venerable Saṃgha listen.

Bhikṣu [Name] has kept several extra robes (*atirekacīvara*), thereby committing an offense of forfeiture and confession (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). The formal act (*karman*) says: "May the venerable Saṃgha listen... [and so forth].
This robe has already been relinquished to the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha shall take this robe and give it to [Name] bhikṣu.

[Name] bhikṣu shall then return it to this bhikṣu. Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha taking this robe and giving it to [Name] bhikṣu, so that [Name] bhikṣu may return it to this bhikṣu, remain silent. Whoever does not consent, speak. The Saṃgha...
The Sangha has consented. This robe is given to [Name] bhikṣu. [Name] bhikṣu shall return it to [Name] bhikṣu.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding those who are to be dealt with immediately: if the offense committed is not one of the five major categories, it should be dealt with according to this method.

Furthermore, if the offense is one of the five major categories but there is no extenuating circumstance and the offender wishes to travel far away, they may postpone the matter until the following day;
it shall likewise be dealt with according to this method. Within the Saṃgha, a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) is made, saying: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. [Name]..."
If a bhikṣu intentionally sleeps apart from his saṃghāṭī robe, he commits an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).

Having forfeited this robe to the Saṃgha, if the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent: I now take this robe and return it to [Name] bhikṣu. The formal motion (*jñapti*) is thus;
the subsequent ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) may be understood by analogy with the above.
The Method for Discarding an Extra Robe by Confession Before Four or Fewer Monks: One should assume the proper dignified demeanor and say: "May the Venerable Ones listen to me.
I, Bhikṣu [Name], have intentionally kept an extra robe for some time and have thus committed an offense requiring forfeiture. I now forfeit it to the Venerable Ones.
Having made this forfeiture, one requests a master of confession; the text for this is as before. The person receiving the confession should then question the others.
The bhikṣu says: "Venerable Elders, if you three Elders would permit me to accept the confession of the bhikṣu [Name], I shall accept it.
They reply: "So be it. The one receiving the confession then informs the bhikṣu:

"So be it. The text for confessing the offense is as before. Regarding the returning of the robe or its value, he makes this formal announcement: "May the Venerable Ones listen. That bhikṣu [Name]..."
"I have kept several extra robes and have thus committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. I have already relinquished these robes to the venerable ones.
Now, may the venerable ones grant me permission to take this robe back to [Name] bhikṣu; I shall then return it. He replies, saying: "So be it."
It may be so. Regarding the ritual for relinquishing robes before a single person: assume the proper dignified demeanor and say: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], have intentionally kept an extra robe for some time and have thus committed an offense involving forfeiture. I now hold this forth and relinquish it to you, Venerable sir. Having said this...
Having relinquished it, one requests the master of confession. The procedure is as before. For the actual method of confession, one says: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, [Name], a bhikṣu, intentionally kept several extra robes and thereby committed an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
These robes have already been relinquished to you, Venerable sir. As for the numerous *pāyattika* offenses [incurred], I now confess and reveal them to you, Venerable sir. Do not...
"I dare not conceal it. The remaining phrasing is as before. Regarding the return of the value of the robe, there is no formal announcement (*jñapti*).
The method for repenting minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*): The Buddha said, "If one commits an offense ranging from *saṃghāvaśeṣa* down to *duṣkṛta*, and knowingly conceals it..."
One should first instruct [the offender] to perform a *duṣkṛta* confession. Now, according to the rules on forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), there are eight categories of *duṣkṛta* offenses.
The first consists of two fundamental categories: namely, wearing the forfeitable robe and failing to disclose it when questioned during the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
Next are six derivative categories; the first two of these are: namely, concealing a *pāyattika* offense for one night, and [concealing it for more than one night].
When one night has already passed, there are two subsequent categories: namely, concealing an attachment to a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* robe, which has been kept for one or two nights.
Following these are two further categories: namely, concealing the failure to confess after being questioned during the *poṣadha*, which has been kept for one or two nights.
Together with the root offenses from which they arise, these constitute eight categories in total.
Now, first, one shall repent for the six minor offenses committed since birth. Assuming the proper dignified demeanor, one addresses the presiding master of confession, saying:
"Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], a bhikṣu, intentionally retained several extra robes, thereby committing numerous *pāyattika* offenses.

I concealed them overnight, and as the nights passed, I continued to conceal them. Furthermore, I wore and used these robes subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), thereby incurring *duṣkṛta* offenses."
I have committed a *pārājika* offense. Having concealed it for one night, I continued to conceal it for subsequent nights.
When the Sangha recited the *Prātimokṣa*, I remained silent and spoke falsely, committing a *duṣkṛta* offense. Having concealed this for one night, I continued to conceal it for subsequent nights;
I have committed countless *duṣkṛta* offenses in this manner. I now disclose and repent before the Venerable One. I shall not dare to do so again. May the Venerable One bear this in mind.
"I. [The remaining phrasing is the same as before.

Next, one shall repent for the two minor offenses that constitute the root transgressions. Assuming the proper deportment, one addresses the presiding master of confession, saying: "Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, Bhikṣu [Name], have committed the offense of wearing impure robes and have committed a false silence during the recitation of the Prātimokṣa; I have committed both offenses."
Regarding the *dukkaṭa* offenses, I do not recall their number individually. I now disclose and repent them before the Venerable One. I dare not commit them again.
May the Venerable One bear me in mind. The remaining words are the same as before.
The method for confessing a *pāyattika* offense. This dharma involves no material object to be relinquished; it consists solely of requesting confession. It comprises three parts:

requesting the presiding confessor (*pratideśanā-ācārya*), the formal act of confession, and the conclusion. The text is largely identical to that of the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, though the specific matters differ.
These are merely changes of terminology according to the specific circumstances. As for the eight grades of minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*), one may exercise self-judgment;
should one commit any of them, the confession is performed exactly as before, with the only difference being the alteration of the name and characteristics of the offense.
Regarding the *pāṭidesanīya* dharma of confession, one should request a single person to serve as the presiding master for the confession.
The wording of the request is the same as before, with the only difference being the change of the name of the offense. Next, perform the formal confession.

Assuming the proper deportment, he says: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], have committed a *pāyattika* offense due to a certain matter, the number of which I do not recall.
Venerable sir, I have committed a blameworthy act that ought not to have been done."
Now, one should repent before the Venerable One. The person receiving the confession should say: "Do you see your transgression? He should answer: "I see it.
[The recipient] should reprimand him, saying: "Be careful not to commit it again. He should answer: "I shall receive and uphold this with the highest reverence."
Regarding the method for repenting *duṣkṛta* offenses, the Buddha said:
"If one commits it intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense that must be repented; this is because one has committed a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*anācāra*).
If one does not commit it intentionally, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* offense. For one who acts intentionally, first assume the proper demeanor and request [the preceptor to perform the ritual]."

The presiding master of confession says: "Virtuous One, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], a bhikṣu, request the Virtuous One to act as my presiding master for the confession of a *duṣkṛta* offense.
May the Virtuous One, out of compassion, act as my presiding master for the confession of this *duṣkṛta* offense.
After the three requests have been made, one should perform the confession for both the derivative and the fundamental offenses, while also carefully examining their specific characteristics.
To whatever extent [the offense has occurred], one should then address the master of confession, saying: "Virtuous One, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, [Name], have intentionally worn the saṃghāṭī robe in a disordered manner, thereby committing an indefinite number of *duṣkṛta* offenses. I now disclose and confess these before the Virtuous One;
I shall not dare to do so again. May the Virtuous One bear this in mind for me. The remaining words are the same as before. If it was done inadvertently, one should...

Maintaining dignified deportment, with a sense of shame and remorse arising in the mind, one says: "I, [Name], a bhikṣu, have mistakenly committed the offense of wearing the saṃghāṭī-cīvara in an untidy manner.
I have incurred a duṣkṛta offense. Today I reproach my own heart and repent of this transgression. Having spoken once, he should stop.
These aforementioned six types are collectively termed the "six groups" (*ṣaḍ-varga*). If *sthūlātyaya* is not separately enumerated, they are simply called the "five categories.
If, within the category of *duṣkṛta*, one distinguishes between *duṣkṛta* (wrong doing) and *durbhāṣita* (wrong speech), they are then called the "seven groups.
Regarding these, an offense committed through speech is termed *durbhāṣita*; an offense committed through bodily action is termed *duṣkṛta*.
The method of repentance is explained in detail within the Vinaya; one should practice according to it, for this alone extinguishes the offense of violating the precepts.

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Although the rules in the Vinaya may be extremely minute, through repentance they become pure. However, if one merely violates the ten wholesome precepts (*daśakuśala-karmapatha*), even though one repents, rebirth in the three evil realms is not eliminated.
This is like the case of violating the fundamental precepts (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). One must know that in such cases, one should rely on Mahāyāna methods of repentance.
Regarding the Dharma, there are generally two types. First is the ritual repentance (*sāṃghāṭī-pratikramaṇa*). As the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:
"Recite the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts during the six periods of day and night; with utmost sincerity, prostrate to the Buddhas of the three periods.

Furthermore, one should diligently practice the repentance rites of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the *Mahākaruṇā Sūtra*, and others; these will certainly extinguish transgressions. Second is the rational repentance (*tattva-pratikramaṇa*). As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If..."
There are those who cultivate the body, ethical discipline, the mind, and wisdom, and are able to contemplate all phenomena as being like empty space.
Even if they have committed evil deeds, through contemplation and investigation, they can transform heavy retributions in the hells into light experiences in the present life.

If, however, one cannot emerge from even minor offenses, and their mind lacks initial repentance such that they are unable to practice virtue and conceal their flaws, then although they possess virtuous karma, it is defiled by the stains of sin.
To commit such defilements and receive light retribution in the present life, yet transform it into the extremely heavy evil fruits of hell—this is called folly.
If one commits the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, or slanders the Dharma, this is termed "breaking the precepts. However, if there is a causal condition, one may still be rescued.

If one dons the dharma robes, constantly maintains a sense of shame and remorse, gives rise to the mind that protects the Dharma, and establishes the True Dharma—I say that such a person is not called one who has broken the precepts.
Regarding the precepts, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "For one who possesses the notion of a self (*ātman*), karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) accumulate;

if there is no self, then various karmas cannot bring about retribution, as the necessary conditions are incomplete. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "It is like a magician who can deceive the eyes of people;
all karmas are likewise. This is called the pure and true repentance (*deśanā*). Repentance for prior deeds merely suppresses karma; [the latter...]
Ritual repentance alone can directly sever karmic obstructions; when ritual and principle are cultivated together, they are like the two wheels of a chariot—nothing remains beyond reach.
Thus one may emerge from the sea of suffering and proceed to the site of enlightenment; how could it be merely for the extinction of transgressions?

Regarding the requisites for the causes of Buddhahood, the Buddha saw various bhikṣus traveling on the road, all carrying their robes as heavy burdens. He desired to establish a regulation.

At that time, during the first watch of the night, he sat in the open air wearing a single robe. Reaching the middle watch of the night, feeling cold, he put on a second robe. Reaching the last watch of the night, again...
Feeling cold, he put on the three robes (*tricīvara*). Thereupon, he had this thought: "In the future, bhikṣus shall be permitted to keep three robes;
these will suffice to ward off the cold, and they must not be kept in excess. Furthermore, one day the Buddha left the city of Rājagṛha and traveled south to the front of the cave of Kāśyapa.
Seeing that the furrows of a watered field were perfectly aligned, he looked back and said to Ānanda: "The appearance of the robes of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time is like this."
It was so. Thereupon, he commanded Ānanda to instruct the bhikṣus on how to make this robe, saying:
"You must know that this is a long strip, this is a short strip, this is a leaf, this is a seam, this is the first seam, this is the second seam, and this is the central seam.

This is a robe with strips and leaves facing both ways; the characteristics of the strips must be equal. As for the 'rice paddy field' pattern, it is a metaphor for the way this robe gives rise to various [features]."
It is a field of merit for the world. That which is produced by cutting with a knife cannot be plundered by enemies or thieves.
It is permitted to make an *antarvāsa* (inner robe) four cubits long and two cubits wide; it is permitted to make an *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe).
The *saṃghāṭī* is five cubits in length and three cubits in width; the measurement of the cubit is not fixed. The Buddha said: "It should be according to the proportions of one's own body.
The leaves [of the robe] must be at most four finger-widths wide and at least as narrow as a grain of barley.

One must fold back the edges before sewing, either using a horse-tooth stitch or a bird-foot stitch, so that dust and grime do not enter within. Any place where there is no seam is called a "window" (*vivaṭa*).

A "hole" (*kōng*) refers to a drainage aperture in a field plot from which water flows out. One should apply a binding seam (*yán*) four finger-widths wide and provide a loop (*jiū*) eight finger-widths behind it.

Even if the three robes (*sāṃghāṭī*, *uttarāsaṅga*, and *antarvāsaka*) are torn, as long as the binding seams remain intact, one does not lose the formal possession (*parigraha*) of them. If they are damaged, one should patch them according to the size and shape of the hole, even if it is only two finger-widths large.
If one enters a village or a layperson's dwelling without wearing the three robes, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. Entering such places without the robes is likewise a violation.
If one does not fasten the buttons, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense at every house. If the lower part of the robe is damaged, one may wear it inverted with the hooks and buttons placed below.

When traveling on the road, for the sake of protecting the folds of the robe, one is permitted to enter a village wearing it on the back; however, upon reaching the place where the bhikṣu is, one must put it on correctly.
The robe and bowl should always follow him, like the two wings of a bird. This is as when seeing the Buddha, paying homage to the Buddha, or inquiring after his well-being—[these are the two].

When the Master enters the assembly and so forth, he should bare his right shoulder. If he is invited for a meal, or when practicing meditation, reciting the scriptures, or entering a village, he should cover both shoulders to manifest the appearance of a field of merit.
The three robes are collectively termed *kāṣāya*. Originally, *kāṣāya* was the name of a plant whose dye could be used for clothing;
thus, the name of that grass was applied to designate these garments. Various masters have offered numerous translations, all of which are interpretive (*yìfān*) rather than literal (*zhèngfān*).
Their substance is made of woven cloth; animal fur or silk cocoons are not appropriate. As for their color, three types of "defiled" colors (*huài-sè*) are used. Five...
A superior color is not appropriate. If one makes robes from cloth obtained through forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*) or acquired through wrong livelihood, they do not constitute valid acceptance.
For the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), the limit is five days; for the seven-piece robe (*saptaka*), the limit is four days; for the five-piece robe (*pañcaka*), the limit is two days.
Should these limits be exceeded, a nun commits a *pāyattika* offense, and a monk commits a *dukkaṭa* offense. If the robe is completed but not formally accepted (*parigṛhīta*), it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Dulva (Vinaya) states:

The sūtras say that the *kāṣāya* is the emblem of the noble ones. One who follows the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*) with a mind of compassion, yet has not yet attained the conduct of a *śramaṇa*, should give rise to faith and respect for the *kāṣāya* through eight considerations:
first, one should conceive of it as a stūpa; second, one should conceive of it as tranquility.

1. One should form the perception [of the Buddha]. 2. One should form the perception of the Dharma. 3. One should give rise to the perception of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). 4. One should give rise to the perception of compassion (*karuṇā*). 5. One should give rise to the perception of [the teacher] as being like the Buddha.

6. One should give rise to the perception of shame (*hrī*). 7. One should give rise to the perception of dread of blame (*apatrāpya*). 8. One should give rise to the perception: "May I, in future lives, be free from the three poisons and be endowed with the conduct of a śramaṇa."
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: When the Buddha made his vow before the Buddha Ratnagarbha, he prayed: "When I attain Buddhahood, may my *kāṣāya* possess five kinds of merit.

First, those who have committed grave offenses or held wrong views upon entering my Dharma—if they should for even a single thought-moment feel reverence and respect [for this robe], they shall certainly receive a prediction of enlightenment within the Three Vehicles.
Second, whether devas, nāgas, humans, or ghosts, if they can show even a small measure of respect for this *kāṣāya*..."
First, one immediately attains non-retrogression in the three vehicles. Second, if there are ghosts or spirits, people shall obtain the *kāṣāya* robe;

even if it is only four inches in size, their food and drink will be fully provided. Third, if sentient beings are in mutual conflict, by recollecting the power of the *kāṣāya*, they will immediately give rise to a mind of loving-kindness. Fourth, [the same applies].
Fifth, if one holds even a small portion of the *kāṣāya*, one will always surpass others through respect and veneration.

The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: "Whether one's nature is that of a śramaṇa or whether one defiles the conduct of a śramaṇa, as long as one is a śramaṇa in form who wears the *kāṣāya*, one shall attain nirvāṇa without remainder upon reaching the realms of Maitreya Buddha up to Ruci Buddha."
The commentary states: "Receiving the prohibitive precepts is the nature of a śramaṇa; shaving the head and donning dyed robes is the form of a śramaṇa.

In the *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, the Nāga King addressed the Buddha, saying: "In this ocean there are countless species of nāgas, and there are four garuḍas who constantly come to seize and devour them.
We pray that the Buddha will protect us and grant us peace and happiness. Thereupon, the Buddha removed the garment he was wearing on his body.
Wearing black robes, he addressed the Dragon King, saying: "Take these robes and distribute them among all the dragons, ensuring they reach every one of them.
Even those who receive but a single thread shall not be harmed by the Golden-Winged Bird King; furthermore, whatever those who uphold the precepts desire shall surely be attained."
Chan Master Yongming Shou said: "In the past, the Bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā was once an entertainer who donned the *kāṣāya* to perform as a play.
By virtue of this merit, she now encountered Śākyamuni Buddha and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
If even one without sincere faith can obtain the fourth fruit, how much more so for those with utmost sincerity?"
The Vinaya states: there are four circumstances under which one may travel to another country without wearing the *kāṣāya* without incurring offense. First, where there are no stūpas or monasteries;
second, where there are no bhikṣu-saṃghas; third, where there are robbers and thieves; and fourth, where the king does not favor the Way.
The *antarvāsa* is also called the *antarvāsa-vastra*; this is translated as "inner-layered garment" or "work-garment.
It is four cubits in length and two cubits in width. It consists of five strips, one long and one short, and may be made by cutting and patching or by sewing leaves together.
It may also be made with pleats or plain folds. A new robe consists of a single layer; an old one consists of two layers.
There are four types of formal robes (*cīvara*): namely, the cut-and-sewn (*khaṇḍa*), the patchwork (*saṃghāṭī*), the pleated, and the plain-folded.

Regarding the twenty-two types of robes derived from these, there are two—namely, the cut-and-sewn and the patchwork—which differ according to whether they are worn as upper or lower garments and their respective variations in size. Whether for performing laborious tasks or traveling on the road...
Conversely, when one is about to sleep, one should fold this robe. [In the case of] a deficiency, one may take the two upper robes as the *anugata* (secondary) robes.
The ritual for receiving them is as follows: "Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], receive this five-piece *antarvāsa* robe."

One long and one short; [this] patched robe is to be maintained. Recite this three times. If it is a patch-leaf or a pleated-leaf robe, then change the two characters "ge-zie" (cut) to "tie-ye" (patch).
The ritual for relinquishing is as follows: "Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [so-and-so], this *antarvāsa*, is among my three robes;
having previously accepted and maintained it, I now relinquish it. Recite this once. The same applies to the two upper robes. It may be done thus.
Understand this. If a bhikṣu living alone has an exchange among his three robes, he should maintain proper deportment, take the robe in hand, and with mental reflection and verbal declaration say:
"I, the bhikṣu [Name], now relinquish this five-piece lower robe (antaravāsa)."
Recite this three times. The acceptance is also as before. One should say with mind and mouth: "I, the bhikṣu [Name], now accept this five-piece *antarvāsa* robe.
Recite this three times. The other two robes may be understood by analogy with this. If it is a seamless robe (*sāṇa*), the procedure is the same.
Regarding the formal act of receiving (*pratigraha*): one does not state the specific characteristics of the robe, but simply says, "I now accept and maintain this *kaṭhina-antarvāsa*.

Regarding the formal act of relinquishing (*utsarga*): one simply says, "I now relinquish this *kaṭhina-antarvāsa*. All other wording is identical to that used for the formal acts of receiving and relinquishing robes; it should be understood accordingly.
The *uttarāsaṅga*—also called the *uṭṭarāsaṅga*—is known as the "upper garment" or the "garment for entering the assembly.
It is five cubits long and three cubits wide. When made from seven strips of cloth, it may be either cut (into pieces) or sewn with patches. If it is new, it should be single-layered;
if it is old, it should be double-layered. There are two types of formal robes: those that are cut and those that are patched. From these garments [the following categories arise].
There are twenty-two types; these are also cut and pieced, differing in their dimensions above and below.

Whenever one enters the assembly—to listen to lectures, perform repentance rituals, pay homage to the Buddha, practice seated meditation, observe the *poṣadha*, or during the *pravāraṇā*—one must wear this robe.
As for the missing parts: the *kaṭhina* is made by joining the upper and lower robes together; the methods for its acceptance and relinquishment are the same as before.
The *saṃghāṭī*—also called *saṃghāṭi*, which means "repeated robe" or "patchwork robe"—is five cubits long and three cubits wide.
It should be four inches larger than the seven-robes (*saptaka*). It consists of nine, eleven, or thirteen strips.

Each has two long strips and one short strip; this is called the inferior grade (*hīna-varga*). Fifteen, seventeen, and nineteen strips—each having three long and one short strip—are called the middle grade (*madhya-varga*).
Twenty-one, twenty-three, and twenty-five strips—each having four long and one short strip—are called the superior grade (*adhimātra-varga*).
For new robes, there are two layers; for old robes, there are four layers. There are ten types of formal robes (*cīvara*).
There are eight types, namely nine varieties each for the *khaṇḍa* (cut-and-sewn) and the *patra-puṭaka* (patched-leaf). Regarding robes, there are six types:
two varieties of the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*) and four varieties of the five-strip robe (*pañcaka*).

Whenever entering a royal palace, entering a village, receiving offerings, preaching the Dharma, paying homage to the Triple Gem, or paying homage to one’s preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or teacher (*ācārya*), one should don this robe. [The text here] is missing; it was opened and brought down [from storage].
The procedure for making the two robes is as follows; their acceptance and relinquishment are the same as before.
The Buddha said: "There are five circumstances under which one may keep the saṃghāṭī robe: first, where there is suspicion or fear; second, when it rains."
Third, there is doubt that it will rain. Fourth, the *saṃghāṭī* has not yet been completed. Fifth, washing and dyeing.

Regarding the *antaravāsaka* and the two upper and lower robes made of uncut cloth: some say they are "unsewn strips. To say "uncut" means it consists of a single piece of cloth without being cut into sections;
thus, it lacks the characteristic of a "water-field" (the grid pattern). This [robe] is for the *śikṣamāṇā*, *śrāmaṇera*, and *śrāmaṇerī*.

Regarding the receiving of robes: the measurement of the upper robe is the same as that of the seven-piece robe (*sāṭīka*), and it is used according to the rules for the seven-piece robe. The measurement of the lower robe is the same as that of the five-piece robe (*pañcaka*), and it is used according to the rules for the five-piece robe.
The procedures for receiving and relinquishing them are the same as before; the only difference is that one refers to the three names, such as *śikṣamāṇā*, etc.
Lately within the monastic communities, there has been a total lack of recognition for this robe;
instead, the three robes of a full monk have been directly bestowed upon śrāmaṇeras. This error is profound indeed.
*Saṃkakṣikā* is also called *saṃghāṭī* and *saṃghāṭi*; this is translated as "arm-pit-covering robe. As the Vinaya states:
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī walked about with her chest and shoulders exposed. When a layperson saw this, he criticized and disparaged her, and reported it to the Buddha.

The Buddha then prescribed the saṃkakṣikā (a shawl for covering the shoulders). Therefore, when a bhikṣuṇī receives the full precepts, in addition to being given the three robes, she is further provided with these two garments according to the rule.
A śikṣamāṇā and a śrāmaṇerikā may also receive them. The saṃkakṣikā is two cubits long and [one cubit] wide.
