It shall be four cubits in length. It is used to cover the left shoulder while leaving the right open; it is received by joining the palms. One says: "Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have made this saṃkakṣikā in accordance with the Dharma; I now receive and maintain it. This is said three times. To relinquish it, one says:
Sister, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], this saṃghāṭī is among my five robes;
having previously accepted and maintained it, I now relinquish it. (Recite once. The method for accepting and relinquishing by śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs is the same, differing only in their names.
The shoulder-covering robe (kaṭhina-vastra), also called *gocara* (or *kūśula*). Among the thirteen requisites, its name corresponds to the *saṃkakṣikā*.
This robe and the *saṃkakṣikā* must not be worn together; when one wears the *saṃkakṣikā*, one does not wear this. Its length and breadth are not specified in the received texts.
The *shefa* (abandonment garment) is also modeled after the *śīrṣaka* (shoulder-cloth) and the *pianshan* (partial-sleeve robe);

it was not originally ordained by the Buddha. During the Wei period, when monks were invited into the palace for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, the palace ladies saw that the monks’ arms were exposed and did not consider this appropriate.
They subsequently fashioned garments and offered them as gifts, which were then sewn onto the left side of the *śīrṣaka*. Consequently...
The *shoucheng* (receiving robe) is called so because the *saṃkakṣikā* (undergarment) was worn on the left shoulder and the *pāṭa* (outer robe) was worn on the right shoulder;
later generations combined these two, and they were collectively named the *shoucheng*.
The *niśīdana* is translated as "sitting mat. Formerly, one day the Buddha was touring the various quarters and saw that many bedding items had been damaged.
Because it was defiled by impurities, the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) was prescribed to serve as a barrier for the body, a barrier for the robes, and a barrier for the bedding.

Initially, it was prescribed to be four feet long and three feet wide. Later, because Kālodāyin had a large physical stature, when he saw the Buddha approaching, he pulled the *niṣīdana* toward himself with his hand.
The Buddha asked, "For what reason? He replied, "I wish to make it large. Thereupon, the Buddha [revised the rule].
Increase by half a *vitasti*. Now, it shall be according to the measurement of the body; where it may be added, let it be added. For new cloth, two layers; for old cloth, four layers.
It must not be made as a single layer, nor used in a mixed manner, nor given away as a pure gift (*śuddhadāna*), nor kept overnight apart from the wearer.

If one stays overnight [separated from one's sitting mat], one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*. It need not be relinquished. The Buddha prescribed that when using new requisites, one should place them upon old ones;

if there are no old ones, then that is sufficient. When the Buddha first established the rule, the corner of the *kāṣāya* was to be placed on the left arm, and the sitting mat was to be placed beneath the *kāṣāya*.
Later, young bhikṣus of handsome appearance entered the city to beg for alms, and many...

Out of affection for women, he arranged the corner of his robe to remain on the left shoulder. Later, when the corner of the robe was blown about by the wind, he permitted them to use a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) to weigh it down.
Subsequently, the non-Buddhist Dharmatrāta asked, "Monk, what is the purpose of that piece of cloth held over your shoulder?
He replied, "It is intended to be used as a seat. Dharmatrāta said, "If this robe is so precious," [he continued].
He possessed great majestic power. How could one sit upon the cloth used for sitting? The bhikṣu was unable to respond and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha then prescribed that one should instead place the corner of the robe on the left arm, with the sitting mat beneath the robe;

however, the pointed corners must not hang down in shapes resembling an elephant’s trunk or a sheep’s ear. Regarding the method of receiving [the sitting mat], it says: "Venerable One, with a single mind..."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], reflect: this *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) has been made according to the prescribed measure; I now accept and maintain it. Regarding the *pātra*:
this is translated as "the vessel of the prescribed measure," which is the common utensil for food.

Among the ninety-six types of people, both monastics and laypeople, all possess a *pātra*. However, worldly people mostly use bowls made of various precious materials, copper, tin, wood, stone, and so forth.
Moreover, their construction is uniquely distinct. Those currently used by the śramaṇas consist only of two types: iron and earthenware.
Their form was fashioned by the World-Honored One himself from clay and fired; it is not something common to all people, but rather the emblem of the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Regarding their measurements, the *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra* states: "The upper bowl is one *dǒu*, and the lower bowl is five *shēng*. [I] fear...
People today are unable to receive and maintain [the precepts]. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The capacity is three *sheng* of the Qin measure.
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "The bowl's capacity is one and a half *sheng*; if it exceeds three *sheng*, the receiving and maintaining [of the precepts] is not accomplished.

Judging by this, the explanation in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is correct. Regarding its color, it should be fumigated to make it black or red; it is also said that it may be the color of a pigeon or a peacock, but [it must not be other colors].
It may be used for miscellaneous purposes; one should revere it as one's own eyes. When a bhikṣu lowers his bowl, it is equivalent to a bhikṣuṇī raising her bowl.
All five assemblies should together receive and uphold it. The ritual for receiving it is as follows: "Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name]..."

"This *pātra* should be accepted according to the prescribed measure, because it is for constant use. (Recite this) three times. The procedure for the four lower assemblies to receive [the bowl] is also based on this.
If there is no one else present, one may accept the bowl alone; then, maintaining dignified deportment, holding the bowl in hand, one should mentally contemplate and verbally recite:
"I, the bhikṣu [Name], accept this pātra of standard measure for regular use. The procedure for relinquishing it may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

Regarding the *kaṭhina* robe—this is translated as the "robe of merit" (*guṇavastra*) or the "robe of celebration" (*abhinandana-vastra*). It refers to the robe of those who have completed the *pūrvavārṣika* (early summer) retreat.
The summer retreat has already concluded. Because his merit is superior, he is honored with this reward; thus, he receives it on the sixteenth day of the seventh month.
Those who entered the later retreat may not receive it. Furthermore, it is said that "Kārttika" refers here to the Pleiades (Mṛgaśīrṣa);
because the Pleiades are in this month, one obtains robes in this month, and for this reason it is called Kārttika. There are five ways of receiving these robes.

The five privileges (*pañca-vastu-prasāda*) refer to: possessing surplus wealth; staying overnight separated from one's robes; accepting individual invitations; eating separately from the community; and visiting other households before or after the meal.
One may keep such extra robes until the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, at which point they must be relinquished to novices (*śrāmaṇera*) and others.

One then receives the three robes (*tricīvara*) again. These robes have borders on all four sides and consist of five strips (*pañca-paṭṭa*), with each strip divided into ten sections. This is also clearly shown [in the illustrations].

The characteristics of the field: if one obtains a new garment, or a garment offered by a donor, or a *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) that does not belong to a deceased person—provided it is a new item—it must be purified by folding (*saṃstarana*).

If it has already been washed, it must be folded and purified after washing. It must be received on the same day without being kept overnight, and it must not have been obtained through wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
Only then may it be formally accepted and maintained. At the time of receiving and at the time of relinquishing it, the bell must be struck to assemble the Saṃgha.
The *karmavācanā* is fully detailed in the section on the *pravāraṇā*.

Regarding the five types of patched robes (*pañca-paṭapilotika*), they are composed of five kinds of cloth: first, cloth with a donor; second, cloth without a donor; third, cloth obtained through exchange;
fourth, cloth from a corpse; and fifth, refuse rags (*pāṃśukūla*). "Cloth without a donor" refers to that which is discarded by the roadside.
[Examples include] robes, robes discarded by a river, and robes worn through by ants. Regarding "robes for going and returning":

this refers to when Indians whose relatives have died present them with robes to be sent to the forest, and then take them back to offer as gifts to the Saṃgha. The rest may be understood [from the context]. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"There are ten benefits to wearing rag-robes (pāṃsukūla): first, they are counted among coarse garments; second, there is little to be sought after; third, one acts according to one's own will..."
1. It may be sat upon. 2. One may lie down on it at will. 3. It is easy to wash. 4. It contains few insects. 5. It is easy to dye. 6.
It is difficult to destroy. 7. There are no other garments [to compare]. 8. One does not lose the pursuit of the Way. When the patched robe (*nāṃsi*) is completed, its weight is not considered;

whether it is many or few pieces, it need not be formally purified through donation (*viśuddha-dāna*). However, even when the patched robe is finished, it must manifest the appearance of a field (*kṣetra-lakṣaṇa*). If the appearance of a field is not manifested, it is not [a true patched robe].
It is permitted to enter a village wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*).

There are ten kinds in total: namely, cloth gnawed by oxen, cloth bitten by rats, cloth burned by fire, cloth [soiled] by menstrual blood, cloth from a woman who has recently given birth, cloth from a shrine, cloth blown by the wind or carried to another place by birds, cloth from a cemetery, and cloth sought [from such places].
There are ten types of robes: the *cīvara*, the robe for a king’s investiture, and the robe for travel. Taking these to be washed, dyed, and used beyond their proper measure; the rain-bath robe;
and on the day the householder Viśākhā invited the Buddha for a meal, she sent a maidservant to announce that it was time. Just then, a heavy rain began to fall.
The Buddha commanded the community of monks to bathe in the rain. When the maidservant saw them, she thought they were naked heretics and returned [to report this].

She informed her mother, who instructed her to invite [the Buddha] again. The Buddha, together with the assembly of monks, came to attend the meal. When the meal was finished, the mother requested that they be given *varṣāśāṭī* robes for the rainy season retreat.
Consequently, the Buddha established the regulation that they should be six spans in length and two and a half spans in width.
Regarding the wound-covering cloth: initially it was made of coarse cloth, which caused pain when lifted.
The Buddha ordered that it be made of extremely fine cloth, measuring four spans in length and two spans in width.
The *nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī* (also called *nivāsana* or *nivāsana*). Its shape is roughly like the skirt worn here [in this land], though it has no ties or loops.
It reaches to the heart above and down to the ankles below. When putting it on, one gathers the fabric into pleats and secures them with a belt;
the belt is three finger-widths wide and wraps around the waist three times.
*Śalākā*. Translated as "inner garment," it refers to the small *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*. It is worn during manual labor and while sleeping.
The water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*) is an essential item for practicing compassion and protecting living beings; thus, it is included among the six requisites.
Any who have become monks must not be separated from it day or night. Its bottom is made of fine cloth, and its frame is made of iron. When first used for straining...
One must gaze upon it with profound attentiveness. When returning it [to its place], one must strictly avoid causing any damage; for from this, the Great Practice arises.
By all means, do not treat it lightly as a mere trifle.
The *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) is also called the Staff of Wisdom and the Staff of Virtue; it is the emblem of the sages and worthies. Recite the three *dhāraṇīs*.

The sufferings of the three miserable realms, the three calamities, and the three worlds; the four-pronged [vajra] is used to sever the four modes of birth. Within the central shaft, it is five feet high, used to sever the transmigration of the five paths.

The twelve rings represent mindfulness of the twelve links of dependent origination. The three bells and four prongs together total seven, representing mindfulness of the seven factors of enlightenment.
Together with the central shaft, they form eight, representing mindfulness of the eightfold noble path and the removal of the eight difficulties. Above.
The upper portion is made of tin; the middle portion is made of wood; and the lower portion is made of ivory or horn. One should hold it according to the Dharma.
By doing so, one manifests dignified deportment in the present life, which assists in attaining the fruit in the future and swiftly brings about perfect enlightenment.
The Daily Rules for the Teaching on the Method of Handling the Alms Bowl: When about to take up the bowl while ascending the hall, one must first wash the hands.

Wipe the hands on the hand-towel until they are dry, then hold the towel between the middle fingers. Wait for the tolling of the bell to cease, then properly hold the towel and grasp the bowl while reciting this verse: "Grasping..."
Holding the alms-bowl, one should make this aspiration: "May all sentient beings become vessels of the Dharma and receive the offerings of devas and humans.
*Oṃ kili kili vajra hūṃ phaṭ paṭa.* One should hold it with both hands, bringing it down so that the handle points toward the body.
The bowl should not be held too high nor too low; the proper measure is at the level of the chest. Upon reaching the destination...
At the place where one sits, first lay down the cloth and then the bowl. The bowl must always be kept away from the knees and the cloth; one must not rest the hands upon the knees.
One must not tilt the bowl so that remaining drops fall onto the floor in front. Spread out the bowl and recite this verse:
"The Tathāgata’s vessel of appropriate measure, I now spread it out; may I, together with all beings, equally realize the emptiness and stillness of the three spheres."
Oṃ smara maṇi svāhā. Whenever one receives food, the bowl or alms-basin must be kept off the bed.
When mindful of making the offering, the right hand’s thumb and ring finger are joined, and the left hand holds the bowl level with the eyebrows to present it.

The ritual text is as usual. The visualization for generating the offering is as follows: "The power of the Dharma is inconceivable; compassion is without obstruction. Seven grains [of rice] pervade..."
To the ten directions. Universally bestowed throughout the entire *sāhasra-lokadhātu*. Oṃ ture svāhā. The attendant delivers the food. Recite:
"O hosts of spirits and deities, I now bestow this offering upon you. This food pervades the ten directions; may all spirits and deities share in it.
Oṃ murliṅga svāhā. Ring the finger-snap three times. The midday meal is the same as this; it need not be repeated.
Set aside other thoughts and recite the verses and mantras. The *Sengba* (Monastic Code) states: "The Buddha ordained that bhikṣus maintain five reflections while eating.
To scatter the mind with idle chatter makes it difficult to digest the faithful offerings. Upon hearing the sound of the *qing* (gong), each member of the assembly shall maintain right mindfulness.

The attendant strikes the *qing* once, and one should contemplate the five reflections: first, calculate the labor expended and measure the distance from whence the food came; second, reflect upon one’s own virtuous conduct.

One should partake of the alms-food while remaining fully mindful and alert. Third, one should guard the mind to remain free from faults, taking the abandonment of greed and other afflictions as the primary principle.
Fourth, one should properly regard the food as excellent medicine for healing the withered body. Fifth, one should accept this food solely for the purpose of attaining the Way.

When first raising the spoon, one should vow: "May all evil be severed. With the second spoon, one should vow: "May all good be cultivated. With the third spoon, one should vow: "May the roots of goodness thus cultivated be dedicated to all sentient beings."
May all universally attain the Buddha-way. When eating even a single mouthful of rice, one must take it with a single scoop from the spoon and place it directly into the mouth;
the mouth must not be opened too wide. One must not place the food on the napkin before eating.
One must not use the spoon or chopsticks to scrape the bowl or basin, nor make noise while doing so. If any food falls onto the napkin, one must not pick it up to eat.
One should collect [the utensils] and place them in one spot, waiting to entrust them to a *śrāmaṇera*. Whatever remains in the bowl must not be taken back into the room.
After completing the *zhai* (fasting) and reciting the *Cundi-dhāraṇī* or the *Disaster-Dispelling Dhāraṇī*, one should conclude by reciting:
"Those who practice giving will surely obtain its benefit; if one gives for the sake of joy, one will later attain peace and happiness."
Next, he reflects: "The meal is finished; I shall receive the *dakṣiṇā* as usual. Having completed the reflection on the Heart Sūtra, he recites the verse:
"The two gifts of material wealth and Dharma are equal and without distinction; may the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) be fully accomplished."
Exiting the hall: First, lift the edge of the bowl’s rim; ensure the handle of the spoon points toward the body. Hold the bowl at chest level and do not look around.
Upon exiting the hall door, one must walk along one side of the corridor. Entering the hall first follows the same procedure.
Returning to the quarters, one must first soak the bowl in water; one should use a large ladleful of water to soak it in a basin, using *sòjiào* (Gleditsia sinensis) pods.
It may be two inches long. If the bowl-stand is short, one should yield to the senior monk (upādhyāya). One must not place it haphazardly.
When wishing to wash the bowl, one must first gather up one's robes so that they do not touch the ground. To wash the bowl, one should first use clear water once.
Next, use the soap-nut (sāgala) juice from within the bowl and pour it out using the alms-bowl itself. The upper two parts [of the liquid] are considered pure;
the lower one part is considered defiled. Whenever holding the bowl to rinse it, the water must not be poured out too high.

One should bend the waist and lower the head to pour the water, keeping the bowl at a distance of one span from the ground. When washing it with hot water, do so in this manner so as not to damage the luster of the bowl.
If the luster of the bowl is damaged, it will readily retain grease and be difficult to wash. When washing the bowl, hold it seven inches above the ground;
do not let it make a sound. Change the water three times. When discarding the water, do not sprinkle it on the ground. As you discard the water used for washing the bowl, recite this verse:
"I offer this water from my washed bowl, like celestial nectar, to all the spirits and ghosts, so that they may all obtain [its benefit]."
[The bowl] is full. Oṃ maheśvara svāhā. Furthermore, there are seven matters:
first, if there is leftover rice in the bowl, one must not simply take it and discard it. Second, if one wishes to discard the rice from the bowl, one should place it on clean ground.
Third, one should use soap powder or grass leaves [to wash]. Fourth, when washing the bowl...
One should obtain a clean place within the human realm. Fifth, when washing the bowl, one should ensure there is a ledge beneath it. Sixth, one should use fresh water;

one must not discard the wastewater too far away so as to splash others. Seventh, when wishing to discard the water from the bowl, one should hold it four inches above the ground, ensuring that the height remains level throughout.
There are five matters regarding the wiping of the alms bowl: First, one should wash one's hands again and wipe [the bowl] until it is dry.

Second, one should hold a clean hand-towel and place it upon the knees. Third, one should wipe the interior and make it dry. Fourth, once the exterior has been wiped, one must not wipe the interior again.
Fifth, when the bowl is dry, one should immediately take the clean hand-towel, cover [the bowl], and place it in its bag; if it is not yet dry, one should wait for it to become dry. Thus it is said.
If there is urgent business and you must travel, you may wear it during the day; if it becomes damp, dry it by holding it toward a fire.
When begging for alms, the bowl should always remain at your left side. Regarding the etiquette for carrying the bowl: when going out, it should be held with the opening facing outward.
When you have received food and returned, you should place it inside [the bowl]. As you eat, you should perform the ritual prayer of aspiration (*pariṇāmanā*).
When invited to a meal, you must not stir or scrape excessively within the bowl. You must not tap the table with your chopsticks.
You must not privately give food away, such as picking some out to give to a dog. If someone comes to add more food, you must not say, "I do not need it. If you are already full, you should...
He brushed it away with his hand. When eating under a tree, if water was unavailable, he used clean grass to thoroughly wipe the bowl.
When going out, he carried the bowl with him, ensuring the opening of the bowl faced outward; he must not hang the bowl from the top of his staff.
If you encounter a teacher on the road, you should place your alms bowl on clean ground, pay homage, and explain the situation as it is.
Then, take the teacher's bowl and carry it yourself, following behind the teacher.
The Method for Carrying the Śikya Staff: When taking up the staff, receive it from a śrāmaṇera and immediately recite this verse:
"Holding the śikya staff, I vow that all sentient beings shall establish great assemblies of giving and demonstrate the path of reality.
Oṃ kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa ṭha ba ti kṛti naya bha ne hūṃ phaṭ. When walking, wear it on the left [shoulder].
Beneath the armpit, one should secure it with the little finger so that both ends are level and even, without allowing them to be high or low.
When standing, a monk places it upon his left foot, and a nun places it upon her right foot; it must not touch the ground.

When begging for alms, one should approach as few as three houses or as many as seven; if nothing is obtained, one must not exceed this limit. To exceed it is contrary to the Dharma of the practitioner.
If one obtains food within the prescribed time limit, one should hold the staff and hang it upon a tree so that it does not touch the ground.
If there is no tree, place it on a level spot on the ground so that it does not lean or fall over. When sleeping, the staff should be aligned with the body;

place it behind the bed, level with the body, neither protruding forward nor receding back. When resting while traveling, the head of the staff should face the sun; do not let it point in the opposite direction.
To transgress [these rules] while holding a staff constitutes eleven matters: first, because there are insects in the ground; second, because one is aged and infirm;
third, because one has crossed over [a boundary]; fourth, one must not hold the staff in the hand while moving forward or backward; fifth, one must not carry the staff on the shoulder.
1. One must not place [the staff] horizontally over the shoulder with both ends hanging down. 2. When entering or exiting and seeing a Buddha image, one must not allow any sound to be made.
3. One must not enter the assembly while holding a staff. 4. One must not carry it [the staff] to the rear of the quarters.
5. One must not carry the staff past midday and exit. 6. One must not point the staff at people or draw figures or write characters on the ground. 7. There is...
There are four circumstances under which one may go beyond the midday meal limit: first, traveling to a distant invitation; second, visiting the home of a sick person; third, escorting the deceased;
and fourth, being invited by non-Buddhists.

Furthermore, there are five matters: First, when the three masters go out together, one must not carry a staff with oneself. Second, when four people travel together, unless it is the Elder, no one may carry [a staff] at all.
Third, upon arriving at the gate of a donor, one should properly rectify one’s deportment. Fourth, having entered the gate of a donor, one should shake [the robes] three times;
if they do not come out after three attempts, follow them to another house. Fifth, when emerging from begging for food, one should...
When placing the staff, it should rest against the center of the left elbow.
Furthermore, there are five matters: first, the staff must always remain in one's own room and may not be separated from the body; second, it is not permitted to let the lower end touch the ground;
third, it is not permitted to allow clothing to grow on the staff; fourth, it must be polished and wiped clean every day; fifth, regarding the staff...
When leaving, one should receive [permission] from the side of a *śrāmaṇera*; if there is no *śrāmaṇera*, it may also be obtained from a *karmadāna* (pure person).
Descending from the bed, recite this verse: From the morning dawn until evening, all sentient beings have crossed paths beneath my feet;
if any have lost their bodies here, may you all be born simultaneously in the Pure Land. Oṃ yid te lhye ya.
*Svāhā*.

When walking on the road, do not harm insects. Recite this verse: "When lifting the foot, one should wish that all sentient beings emerge from the ocean of birth and death and be endowed with all wholesome dharmas. Oṃ dhiḥ riḥ svāhā."

Chewing the *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-stick), one recites this verse: "When chewing the tooth-stick, I vow that all sentient beings may have minds that are harmonious and pure, and may they devour all afflictions.
Oṃ amuka me mule īvākara saṃśodhane padma kumāra īvasaṃśodhaya dhara dhara sumi maṭi."
*Svāhā*.
When washing the face, recite this verse: "Washing the face with water, I vow that all sentient beings shall attain the gateway of the pure Dharma and be forever free from defilement. Oṃ laṃ svāhā."
Shaving the hair, he recites the verse: "As I shave off my beard and hair, I vow that all sentient beings shall forever be free from afflictions and ultimately attain tranquil extinction.
Oṃ siddhantu mantrapadāni svāhā.
Then he drinks water, reciting the verse: "The Buddha beheld eighty-four thousand insects in a single bowl of water; if one does not uphold this mantra..."
As when eating the flesh of sentient beings: *Oṃ vaśīvara maṇi svāhā*.
For bathing, recite this verse: "When washing the body, one should wish that all sentient beings have no defilement in mind or body, and be radiant and pure within and without.
*Oṃ vajranartaka svāhā*."
Circumambulating the stupa, recite this verse: Circumambulating the stupa, I vow that all sentient beings shall act without opposition and attain all-encompassing wisdom.
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ dūpadūpa svāhā*. When using the toilet, snap the fingers three times and recite this verse:
At the time of defecating or urinating, I vow that all sentient beings shall cast away greed and anger.
Delusion. To eliminate the laws of sin: Oṃ hulu-dhaye svāhā.
[This is] the purification. Recite the verse: When the rite is finished, go to the water and make this aspiration for all sentient beings:
"May they swiftly proceed within the supramundane Dharma. Oṃ ha-na-mi-li-ti svāhā.
Washing the hands, one recites this verse: "With water to rinse the palms, may all sentient beings obtain pure hands to receive and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
Oṃ jvala-kāraye svāhā. [This] removes impurities.
One recites the mantra: "To wash away physical defilements, may all sentient beings become pure, harmonious, and supple, ultimately [free from them]."
[The Mantra for Purifying Defilements]: Oṃ śrīye svāhā ṭaba. Recite this verse:
Excellent is this robe of liberation, This robe of the unsurpassed field of merit. I now receive it upon my head;
May I never be parted from it in birth after birth. Oṃ siddhye svāhā.
Donning the seven-piece robe (*saptaka-cīvara*), recite this verse: "Excellent is this garment of liberation, The field of merit unsurpassed.
I now receive it upon my head; May I wear it in every birth. *Oṃ dhupa dhupa svāhā.* Donning the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), recite this verse:
"Excellent is this garment of liberation, The field of merit unsurpassed. I uphold it as the Tathāgata did."
[Recite] the mantra: *Oṃ mahā-kāpa-paṭa-siddhe svāhā*. Spread out the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*). Recite the verse:
The sitting mat, the *niṣīdana*, Nourishes the sprout of the mind’s nature. Spreading it out, one ascends the ground of the sages;
I uphold this in accordance with the Tathāgata’s command. *Oṃ dambha dambha svāhā*.
Ascending the site of enlightenment, he recited this verse: "If I am to behold the Buddha, I vow that all sentient beings shall attain the unobstructed eye and see all Buddhas.
*Oṃ amṛte hūṃ phaṭ*. At the time of sleep, he recited this verse:
"As I lie down to rest, I vow that all sentient beings shall attain peace and happiness in body, and that their minds shall be free from..."
If there is agitation and disturbance, visualize the wheel of the letter *A* with focused intent and recite it twenty-one times in a single breath. Then lie down on your right side.
This gāthā and dhāraṇī were originally not part of the Vinaya; however, because they are commonly studied within the current Vinaya schools, they are recorded here for practical use.
*Shoujie bianwu* (Discerning Errors in Receiving the Precepts).

Regarding the study of the precepts, since the time of the Great Sage, those who have truly mastered it have been rare. For the most part, errors have been transmitted one after another, with no one recognizing their fallacies;
this has continued for several hundred years. I shall now briefly set forth several points to correct these mistakes.
I announce this to all my fellow students: I wish that you would follow the Buddha’s regulations.
Regarding the entrustment of the three robes to a śrāmaṇera, there was an error. According to the Vinaya, a śrāmaṇera wears only the *maṇḍala-antarvāsaka*.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that one should possess two garments: an upper garment, which should be the *uttarāsaṅga*, and a lower garment, which should be the *antarvāsaka*.
Indeed, within the *Nanshan Suiji Jiemó* (Nanshan’s *Karmavācanā According to Circumstances*), there is also a ritual for śrāmaṇeras receiving the *mañca-antarvāsaka*.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottara-karmavācanā* states: "For those who follow the path of the śramaṇa, the *mañca-strika* (the single-strip robe) is the proper attire; to wear the five-strip robe (*pañcaka*) is truly contrary to the Dharma.
Yet, in the monastic communities of this land today, it is common to bestow the five-strip robe [upon novices]. One does not know from what time this practice originated. If...
According to what is stated in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, even five strips of cloth are not permitted; how much more so three robes?
Lately, those who confer the precepts have directly bestowed the three robes upon śrāmaṇeras all at once. This greatly violates the Buddha’s regulations and is improper.
It is an error for four or more bhikṣus to perform the *karmavācanā* together. According to the Vinaya, when receiving the bhikṣu precepts, one person is initially ordained alone.
Only later, due to the arising of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv āpattayaḥ*) and other circumstances, was it permitted for three people to receive them together.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One must not chant and recite simultaneously so as to cause four people to obtain the full ordination (*upasampadā*) at once. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-ksudraka-vastu*...

The *Shishi* (事) states: "Four persons may not receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) together. Why? Because it is illogical for a non-quorum to perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) on behalf of a quorum.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "In all cases, one must not perform a formal ritual with only four persons.
Yet, later masters, regardless of the number of people present, would all conduct the ritual on a single altar. This corruption originated in the South.
There were originally two ordination platforms in the north; however, because there were many people, they eventually received the precepts at a single platform.
Nevertheless, the ritual protocols for the ordination platform specify only three persons, which makes it clear that having four or more is contrary to the proper ritual.
The nuns’ ordination was mistakenly conducted according to the bhikṣu precepts. In the Vinaya, the bhikṣuṇī precepts differ from those of the bhikṣus;
the questions regarding the impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*) asked during ordination are likewise entirely different, as the matters concerning men and women differ.
In recent years, when masters have preached the precepts, they have instead mixed the nuns into the assembly of bhikṣus for a joint ordination; thus, the women received [the precepts] in this manner.
This refers to the precepts for men. Since the ordination platform was already in disorder, it is not only the nuns who failed to receive the precepts;
all the bhikṣus as well failed to receive them. Reflect on this.
Regarding the improper measurement of robes: according to the Vinaya regulations, the *antarvāsa* (inner robe) is four cubits long and two cubits wide, while the *uttarāsaṅga*...
The *saṃghāṭī* is five cubits in length and three cubits in width; the *saṃghāṭī* is likewise. In recent times, masters have produced small versions of the five-fold robe (*pañcaka-cīvara*).

One does not know who first initiated this, but it is a most arbitrary fabrication. Furthermore, there are those who make the dimensions of the five-fold robe identical to those of the seven-fold robe (*saptaka-cīvara*), which is also not the Buddha’s regulation.
As for the seven-fold robe and the great robe (*mahāsaṃghāṭī*), many are made six cubits in length; since—
If it were more than one cubit long, it could not be draped; thus, it was folded over the left arm. I once asked him the reason for this, and he replied:
"The śrāmaṇera has a shaven head and wears square-cut robes. If they were five cubits long, they would not be square.

I did not realize that the term "square-cut robes" (fāngpáo) was originally not spoken by the Buddha; why such bitter insistence? Moreover, even if they were made five cubits long, what would prevent them from being called so?
How lamentable it is that, while following worldly customs handed down by tradition, people fail to examine their own conduct.

To so lightly discard the robes of deceased monks is an error! According to the Vinaya regulations regarding the robes and bowl of a deceased monk, it is not permitted for the deceased to bestow them themselves.

After death, the Buddha permitted them to be given to the attendant who cared for the sick; however, if the attendant already possesses such items, one may perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) within the assembly.
Grind it into powder and scatter it. However, a robe must be received from another person before it can be worn.
Lately, many masters have claimed that the robes of a deceased monk may not be worn; they instead instruct that such robes be hung upon a tree to rot away. This greatly violates the Vinaya.
Furthermore, the Buddha taught that although a robe may be extremely tattered, it must not be worn [by others] nor should it be lightly discarded. Thus...
It can even serve as a lamp wick and increase the merit of the donor; would it now be appropriate to let it rot and decay?
The householder’s giving of the robe was an error. A householder who has received the five precepts need not wear the formal robe (*kāṣāya*).

However, when receiving the Brahmajāla Precepts or entering a ritual arena (*maṇḍala*), wearing the robe is permitted, provided it is made of single-layered seams rather than cut-and-sewn patches. It must not be a double-layered garment.
It is to be made like the robes of the great *saṃgha*. Therefore, the Buddha said: "This robe has one name, 'the three robes' (*tricīvara*), and it is also called 'secular clothing.

How could it be appropriate to entrust [this] to those with the robes of the great *saṃgha*? Even if one were to manufacture and maintain a single-layered sewn garment, it would still be difficult to conform to the Dharma.
If one sleeps together with wife and children, where would one place this robe? The offense of transgressing the Dharma increases along with the passing days."
To accumulate them is surely not as good as not possessing them at all. Thus, Ciyun cautioned against it in the past, and Yunqi prohibited it later;
how could they have lacked discernment?

Regarding the error of not receiving the training precepts (*śikṣamāṇā-śīla*): The Buddha ordained that a *śrāmaṇerī* who wishes to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) must first receive the two-year *śikṣamāṇā* precepts, so that she may train in the discipline (*vinaya*) of a fully ordained nun (*bhikṣuṇī*), and only thereafter proceed to full ordination.

Therefore, when receiving the full ordination of a nun, after the questions regarding the obstacles and impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*) have been completed, one further asks: "Have you trained in the precepts for two years? She replies: "I have trained."
He asked again, "Is your training in the precepts pure? She replied, "It is pure. He then questioned the other nuns in the same manner, and they all answered likewise.
This indicates that she had not received the *śikṣamāṇā* precepts, and thus could not have obtained the full bhikṣuṇī precepts.
Since she has not received these precepts at all, it is a delusion and error to refer to her as a *śikṣamāṇā*, which implies a woman who wears her hair.
The tradition has degenerated to such an extent that it is truly lamentable.
To arbitrarily alter the ritual text is an error; the method for receiving the precepts is clearly set forth in all the various Vinaya schools.

The original text of the Zhaoqing Ordination Platform has already been embellished by later generations and no longer reflects the original version of Master Dazhizhao. For instance, regarding the inquiry into obstacles and impediments:
There are two errors. Within the three *karmas*, there are three types of errors; those who understand this find it difficult to rely upon them for practice.
Recently, there have been masters who, relying on their own cleverness while having no knowledge of the Vinaya at all, have arbitrarily altered the three robes according to their own whims.

Previously, they were taught and practiced by laypeople; it is unknown from which Vinaya these originated. By the time they reached the ordination platform, many additions had been made to the chanting and recitation.
These delighted the audience and were much like the performances of itinerant entertainers; how could this be considered the standard for propagating the Vinaya?
If one were willing to read through the Vinaya even once, one would naturally recognize its own depravity.
The procedure for ascending the altar is often confused and erroneous. Generally, when one receives the precepts, one first requests the ten masters.

Once the requests are completed, the ten masters ascend the altar and then perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) to appoint the instructor (*śikṣācārya*). The instructor then descends from the altar and positions himself where he is within sight but beyond hearing.

The questions regarding obstacles and impediments are asked. Once the questioning is finished, the candidate ascends the platform and makes a formal announcement to the masters. Having made this announcement, the candidate is then summoned to the platform;
this is the ancient rule, and the *Jie ke* (Precepts Ritual) of Zhaokong follows this same procedure.

In recent years, however, various masters have gathered the candidates together on a single platform to request the ten masters to inquire about obstacles and impediments and to perform the *karmavācanā* for the reception of the precepts—all taking place in one location. However...

To recite the ritual text from beginning to end once more—since this is neither a Buddha-ordained rule nor the established custom of Zhaoking—is it not unclear what kind of standard it would constitute?
Nothing could more severely disrupt the altar rites than this. The wise should examine this for themselves.

In the legal categories of the Vinaya masters, there are two kinds of precepts: first, the natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*). These refer to those whose nature is inherently evil and have been prohibited since antiquity;

the four precepts against killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are examples of these. Second, the prohibitory precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*). These refer to those whose acts are not inherently evil, yet have not [been prohibited] since antiquity...
Prohibitions (*vinaya*): These were first established when the Buddha appeared in the world, such as the single precept against drinking alcohol.
*Karma* (formal ritual acts) has two purposes: first, to accomplish wholesome deeds, such as the establishment of boundaries (*sīmā*) and the conferral of ordination (*upasampadā*);
second, to punish offenses, such as repentance (*pratideśanā*) and disciplinary measures including permanent expulsion (*pārājika*).
Regarding the two types of utensils used by the Saṃgha: first, those for pure use, which are made of porcelain or earthenware; second, those for contact use, which are made of copper or iron.

There are two periods for the dhūta practices: from the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month, and from the fifteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the tenth month.
During these two periods, one should constantly practice the dhūta observances.
There are three types of *karmavācanā* (formal acts): first, the *jñapti-karman*, which refers to a single announcement made once;
second, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, which refers to one announcement followed by one formal act;
third, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, which refers to one announcement followed by three formal acts. These three types encompass all *karman*.
Regarding the three methods of *karmavācanā*: when one person dwells alone, they perform the rite through mental recollection and verbal declaration;

when three or fewer persons dwell together, they perform it by mutual face-to-face announcement; when four or more persons dwell together, they perform it by assembling the community for the *karmavācanā*.
The Vinaya has three names: first, *vinaya*, which is translated here as "well-regulated" (*shan-zhi*) and also as "extinction" (*mie*);
second, *prātimokṣa*, which is translated as "guaranteed liberation" (*bao-jietuo*) and also as "individual liberation" (*bie-jietuo*); third, *śīla*, which is translated as "precept" (*jie*).
Regarding the three mentalities for upholding the precepts: first, weariness with all conditioned phenomena; second, the aspiration to attain Bodhi; and third, compassion for sentient beings.
Regarding the three categories of seniority based on years since ordination (*varṣa*): those from one summer retreat up to nine summers are called junior monks (*navaka*);

those from ten summers up to nineteen summers are called middle-ranking monks (*madhyama*); and those from twenty summers up to forty summers are called senior monks (*sthavira*). Those who have reached fifty summers...
He was known as an elder, revered by all śramaṇas. Regarding food, he avoided the three faults:
first, greed arising from superior flavors; second, anger arising from middling flavors; and third, delusion arising from inferior flavors.
Therefore, he necessarily guarded his mind to remain free from these faults.
The appearance of the light-omen (*āloka-nimitta*) occurs in three stages: first, when the sun first shines upon the Jambū tree, the gods appear black;
second, when the sun shines upon the leaves of the tree, the gods appear blue; third, when the sun shines beyond the tree, the gods appear white.
In the Vinaya it is stated that regarding the appearance of the light-omen, taking the white stage as the definitive standard is correct.
During the *varṣā* retreat, one should avoid three faults: first, wandering about aimlessly, which hinders the cultivation of the path;
second, harming living beings, which deeply violates the spirit of compassion; and third, engaging in improper conduct, which invites public censure.

The funds for bathing the Buddha shall be divided into three portions: one portion is to be used for the Buddha, one portion is to be used for the Dharma, and one portion is to be used for the Sangha;
their use elsewhere is not permitted.

There are four types of preceptors (*upādhyāya*): first, one who possesses the Dharma and provides food and clothing; second, one who possesses the Dharma but does not provide food and clothing; third, one who does not possess the Dharma but provides food and clothing;
fourth, one who neither possesses the Dharma nor provides food and clothing. Of these, the former two types may be relied upon, while the latter two types must not be relied upon.

There are four things that must not be entrusted: first, an elderly person; second, a wicked person from afar; third, great physical strength; and fourth, profit. There are three reasons why one must eat:
first, to provide sustenance for the body so as to cultivate the Path; second, to nourish the parasites within the body; and third, to generate merit for the donor.
Fourth, refuting the Nirgrantha (Jaina) heretics.

There are four kinds of eternalism: first, the eternalism of the eternally eternal, which refers to the monastic community’s kitchen, storehouses, temple buildings, utensils, flowers, fruits, groves, fields, gardens, servants, and livestock.
These may only be used and are not permitted to be divided or sold. Second, the eternalism of the ten directions.

1. *Sthiti* (Abiding): This refers to the regular food provided for the Saṃgha by a monastic community. Its substance extends throughout the ten directions, yet it is restricted to its original location.

3. *Pratyutpanna-pratyutpanna* (Present-before-the-present): This refers to when the Saṃgha receives a gift; since the gift is intended solely for the present Saṃgha of that specific location, it belongs to them alone.

4. *Daśadik-pratyutpanna* (Present-before-the-ten-directions): This refers to light articles belonging to the five groups of renunciants after they have passed away. Before the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) has been performed, these items should be distributed among the present Saṃgha of the ten directions.
Regarding "those who arrive as monks": they all receive a share. However, after the *karmavācanā* has been performed, those from the ten directions who arrive as monks do not receive a share.

There are four types of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*) regarding food: first, "food from the horizontal mouth," which means using crooked flattery toward the powerful and acting as a messenger to the four quarters;
second, "food from the vertical mouth," which means various incantations and divinations of good and bad fortune; third, "food from the upward mouth," which means looking up at... [the heavens].
Astrology; subsisting by these means for one’s livelihood. Fourth, eating from the mouth downward: this refers to cultivating fields and gardens, and compounding medicinal decoctions.
Regarding the four meanings of the Vinaya: first, it is the level ground within the Buddha-dharma, upon which all myriad virtues arise.
Second, all disciples of the Buddha abide by relying on the precepts, and all sentient beings exist by relying on the precepts. Third, it is the path...
It is the primary gateway to *nirvāṇa*. These four are the *maṇi-garland* of the Buddha-dharma, for they are able to adorn the *dharmakāya*.
Regarding the four meanings of *śīla*: first, the meaning of "coolness," because it removes the feverish afflictions of the mind;

second, the meaning of "tranquility," because it serves as the cause for happiness in future lives; third, the meaning of "serenity," because it can establish *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; fourth, the meaning of "quiescence."

Because they serve as the causes for attaining the bliss of nirvāṇa, there are four dhūta practices concerning food: first, eating by alms; second, not performing the *kṛtapiṇḍikriyā* (the ritual of leaving food); third, eating in a single sitting;
and fourth, taking a single mouthful from a single vessel.

The four categories of dhūta practices are as follows: first, regarding clothing, there are two: the patched robe (saṃghāṭī) and the three robes (tricīvara). Second, regarding food, there are two: begging for alms and eating in a single sitting. Third, regarding location, there are three:
the forest hermitage (araṇya), the charnel ground (śmāśānika), and beneath a tree (vṛkṣamūlika). Fourth, regarding constancy, there is one: always sitting (naiṣadyika); these have no fixed sequence.
There are four intentions for begging for alms: first, to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; second, to subdue arrogance; third, to recognize that the body is subject to suffering;
and fourth, to eliminate attachment. There are four ways of dividing the alms:
first, to offer a portion to fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*); second, to give to those who are destitute and begging; and third, to give to the various deities.
1. Ghosts; 2. Eating alone; 3.
Wrong livelihood, which consists of four parts: first, manifesting extraordinary signs for the sake of gain and offerings; second, proclaiming one's own virtues for the sake of gain and offerings;

third, divining good and bad fortune through physiognomy and interpreting it by preaching the Dharma to others; fourth, raising one's voice to display an air of authority so as to inspire fear in others.
Reverence. There are five ways of expressing it so as to receive offerings and move the hearts of others.
The five methods of repentance are: first, baring the right shoulder; second, placing the right knee on the ground; third, joining the palms with a sincere mind.
Fourth, prostrating with the head at his feet; fifth, verbally confessing one's transgressions;
and making offerings to five types of persons: first, one’s father; second, one’s mother; third, one’s preceptor; fourth, one’s instructor; and fifth, the sick.
The Buddha said, "A bhikṣu should serve his parents with all his heart and for the duration of his life. He further stated, "I permit five types of persons;
even if they have utterly violated the precepts, one should still provide them with offerings."

There are five places where one should not frequent: first, the house of an official; second, a tavern; third, the house of a butcher; fourth, the house of a courtesan; and fifth, the house of a caṇḍāla. There are five kinds of ācāryas:
first, the preceptor for ordination (pravrajyā-ācārya); second, the preceptor for the ritual (karmācārya); third, the preceptor for instruction (śikṣācārya).
Fourth is the *śāstrī* (preceptor) for receiving the scriptures; fifth is the *śāstrī* for dependence.
There are five kinds of water filters (*parisrāvaṇa*): first, the square filter made of silk, which may be one or three cubits in size, constructed according to the circumstances.
2. The *dharmaghaṭa* (dharma-jar) is the same as the *yángyīng* (yin-yang jar). 3. To delay the army [of insects], tie the mouth with silk and suspend it in water by a rope;
when full, draw it out. 4. The water-straining cloth (*paryāṅka*) requires only a square handspan of fine silk, which may be tied to the mouth of the jar.
5. One may also strain water using the corner of one’s robe or within an alms bowl.

The five kinds of pure grounds (*śuddhasthāna*) involve the generation of a formal intention (*cittotpāda*). That is to say, when first constructing a monastery, once the foundation has been established, one bhikṣu should generate the intention regarding this monastery:
"One room may be designated as a pure kitchen for the Saṃgha. Second is collective authorization (*sādhāraṇa-parigraha*);
that is, at the time of establishing the foundation, one bhikṣu addresses the assembly of bhikṣus, saying: "Now, venerable sirs, please apply your minds to authorize..."
In this monastery, one room may be designated as a pure kitchen for the monks. Third, "like a cow's lying-down place" (*gośayana*):

this refers to a dwelling within the monastery where the doors of the rooms have no fixed location, resembling a cow's lying-down place; even if the formal ritual has not been performed, such a place may also serve as a pure kitchen. Fourth, "an old abandoned site":
this refers to a long-abandoned monk’s quarters that has been restored, as if returning to what was there before. Upon reaching [such a place], [the ritual may be performed].

The former place of contact is itself pure. Regarding the five methods for establishing the dharma: "making" refers to the assembly collectively determining a specific location to establish the boundary of a pure kitchen by means of a formal motion (*jñapti*) and a second proclamation (*dvitīya-karman*).
A bhikṣu possesses five virtues: first, terrifying Māra; second, being a seeker of alms (bhikṣu); third, pure precepts; fourth, pure livelihood; and fifth, destroying evil.
Regarding the five blessings of observing the fast (upoṣadha), the Buddha said: "Observing the fast for one day provides provisions for six hundred thousand years.
Furthermore, there are five blessings: first, little illness; second, physical ease; third, little lust; fourth, little sleep; and fifth, rebirth in heaven with knowledge of past lives."
In the sutras, whenever the term "fast" (zhāi) is mentioned, it does not merely refer to abstaining from meat, refraining from alcohol, and avoiding the five pungent herbs;
it further entails not eating after midday and ceasing all other evil deeds.
There are five dharmas for entering the assembly: first, one must treat others with kindness, respect, and reverence; second, one should humble oneself as one would a cloth used for wiping dust;
third, one must know the proper timing for sitting, rising, bowing, and looking around; fourth, while among that monastic community, one must not engage in idle chatter.
Regarding the five things that cannot be tolerated, one should likewise remain silent.
There are five kinds of purification for fruit: first, purification by fire; second, purification by the knife; third, purification by a wound; fourth, purification by a bird’s beak;

and fifth, purification by being unfit for planting. These five kinds of purification are permitted for consumption. Among these, purification by the knife, purification by a wound, and purification by a bird’s beak [are specified].
One should eat it after removing the seeds. It is purified by fire; it is not fit for sowing. It is entirely edible. Furthermore, there are five kinds of purification:
if the skin has peeled off, if it is husked, if it is rotten, if it is broken, or if it is shriveled and dried.
There are five faults of sleep: first, bad dreams; second, the failure of the devas to provide protection; third, the mind not entering into the Dharma;
fourth, failing to contemplate the signs of light; and fifth, the tendency toward the emission of semen.
There are five benefits to chewing a *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-stick): first, it provides flavor for every mouthful; second, it removes heat; third, it dispels wind;

fourth, it aids digestion; fifth, it clarifies the eyes. There are five faults of not chewing a tooth-stick: first, the breath smells foul; second, one cannot distinguish flavors; third, phlegm is not cleared away; fourth, [the mouth remains unclean]; fifth, [the teeth become stained].
It does not draw in nourishment; the five eyes are not clear.

There are five faults in eating pungent [vegetables]: first, one’s life-span is diminished; second, the heavens are distant; third, ghosts are near; fourth, blessings are exhausted; fifth, demons gather.
There are five dharmas for entering the homes of laypeople: first, speaking softly upon entering the gate; second, restraining body, speech, and mind; third, maintaining a humble posture;
fourth, properly guarding the sense faculties; and fifth, conducting oneself with dignified decorum so as to inspire joy in others.
Receiving the Bodhisattva precepts yields five kinds of benefits: first, the Buddhas of the ten directions will compassionately regard and constantly protect one;
second, at the time of death, one will possess right view and a joyful mind; third, in every place of rebirth, one will have fellow bodhisattvas as companions.

Fourth, one fully accomplishes the aggregate of merit and the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). Fifth, from now on, throughout future lives, one’s innate ethical nature, merit, and wisdom will be fulfilled.
By not eating after midday, one obtains five kinds of blessings: first, little sexual desire; second, little sleep; third, attaining single-mindedness; fourth...
There is no downward wind. Fifth, his body is at ease and free from illness.
For five reasons, a great bhikṣu manages affairs: first, to repay the Buddha’s kindness; second, to nurture the Buddha-dharma;
third, to eliminate the vulgar and inferior who are self-conceited; fourth, to humble and subdue arrogant disciples in the future; fifth, to inspire and initiate them.
Come, O one of meritorious karma!
There are five things a lay follower (upāsaka) must not do: first, trading in livestock; second, trading in bows, arrows, swords, weapons, and the like;
third, selling liquor; fourth, pressing oil; and fifth, the business of dyeing with the five primary colors. In foreign lands, both oil-pressing and dyeing are included [among these].
It greatly harms the lives of sentient beings; therefore, one should not perform it.

The sixfold harmony of the Saṃgha consists of: harmony in precepts through collective practice, harmony in views through shared understanding, harmony in body through dwelling together, harmony in material gains through equal distribution, harmony in speech through freedom from dispute, and harmony in mind through mutual joy.
A bhikṣu has six articles: first, the saṃghāṭī, here translated as the "double-layered robe"; second, the uttarāsaṅga, here translated as the "upper robe";
third, the antarvāsaka, here translated as the "inner robe"; fourth, the pātra, here translated as the "bowl."
Fifth, the *niṣīdana*, here translated as "sitting mat. Sixth, the *pātrīra-rāvaṇa*, here translated as "water-strainer.
A bhikṣu must keep these six articles with him at all times and may not be parted from them even for a moment.
The seven merits of upholding the Vinaya are: first, being able to uphold the Buddha’s inner treasury; second, being able to skillfully resolve disputes; third, maintaining the precepts;
fourth, standing at the summit of non-Buddhists because of the Vinaya; and fifth, having no fear when preaching the Dharma to the assembly without consulting others.
Sixth, because it is able to sever doubt; seventh, because it is able to cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time.
Eighth, regarding the signs of the extinction of the phenomena of the Teaching: first, a fondness for fine clothing; second, indulgence in idle play; third, slaves becoming bhikṣus;
fourth, slave-girls becoming bhikṣuṇīs; fifth, a lack of interest in the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā); sixth, the slandering of the Vinaya; and seventh—
The *kāṣāya* has turned white and no longer accepts dyeing. Eighth, there is the greedy use of the property of the Triple Gem.
Of these eight matters, the monks and nuns have recently already committed seven; only the *kāṣāya* not turning white remains. Is this not perilous?
The nine kinds of pure meat: first, not killed for one's sake; second, not seen being killed; third, not heard being killed;

fourth, not suspected to have been killed for one's sake; fifth, naturally deceased; sixth, scavenged by birds; seventh, dried while alive; eighth, encountered unexpectedly; ninth, already killed previously.
There are ten benefits to begging for alms: first, one sustains one’s own life; second, one remains independent and does not belong to others;
third, those who give to me sustain their lives through the Three Jewels, and only then may I eat; fourth, it increases compassion; fifth, it accords with the Buddha’s teaching;
sixth, it is easy to satisfy and easy to nourish; seventh, it is the root of merit for those who gaze upon the crown of my head; eighth, when people see me begging for alms...
9. Others shall follow my example. 10. One does not give to men or women, whether young or old, due to various circumstances.
10. One begs for alms in successive order to generate a mind of equanimity.
Regarding the ten dharmas of begging for alms: first, to gather and sustain all sentient beings; second, to beg in successive order; third, to be free from weariness; fourth...
1. Contentment; 2. Distribution [of wealth]; 3. Non-indulgence; 4. Knowing the proper measure; 5. Bringing wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*) to manifestation;
6. The perfection of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*); 7. Freedom from self-grasping (*ātmagrāha*).
There are ten benefits of gruel: first, beauty; second, strength; third, longevity; fourth, happiness; fifth, clarity of speech; sixth, eloquence; seventh, the digestion of food consumed overnight;
eighth, the alleviation of wind-disorders; ninth, the cessation of hunger; and tenth, the quenching of thirst.
There are ten faults of drinking alcohol: first, one's complexion becomes ugly; second, one becomes base and inferior; third, one's vision becomes blurred;
fourth, one manifests signs of anger and resentment; fifth, one ruins one's fields, businesses, and means of livelihood; sixth, one brings about illness; seventh, one increases strife and litigation;
eighth, one's ill repute spreads abroad; ninth, one's wisdom diminishes; and tenth, after death, one falls into the evil realms.
By refraining from killing, one attains ten kinds of merit: first, one attains fearlessness toward all sentient beings;
second, one develops a heart of great compassion for sentient beings; third, one severs evil habitual karma; fourth, one has few illnesses; fifth, one enjoys a long life;
sixth, one is protected by non-human beings; seventh, one has no bad dreams; eighth, one has no enemies; ninth, one does not fear the evil realms; tenth, at the end of life, one is reborn in...
The Noble Path: Thirteen Requisites. First, the *saṃghāṭī*, that is, the great robe (*mahākāṣāya*). Second, the *uttarāsaṅga*, that is, the seven-piece robe.
Third, the *antarvāsa*, that is, the five-piece robe. Fourth, the *niṣīdana*, that is, the sitting mat. Fifth, the lower garment (*śāṭī*).
6. An inner skirt; 7. A *saṃkakṣikā*, that is, an armpit-covering garment; 8. A secondary *saṃkakṣikā*, that is, a *kūrmara*;
9. A body-wiping cloth; 10. A face-wiping cloth; 11. A shaving garment; 12. A wound-covering garment; 13.
A garment for medicinal requisites.
There are thirteen kinds of faults in eating meat: first, that all sentient beings have been one's own parents since beginningless time;

second, that the lives of sentient beings are no different from one's own; third, that it injures the mind of compassion; fourth, that it increases the karma of killing; fifth, that it increases the karma of debt;

sixth, that it increases the habitual tendencies of a rākṣasa; seventh, that it accumulates defilement and turbidity; eighth, that it renders the recitation of sūtras and the worship of the Buddha [ineffective].

1. They possess no merit whatsoever. 2. Those who study and maintain mantras and mudrās will achieve nothing. 3. The devas will distance themselves daily. 4. Malevolent spirits will draw near daily. 5.
When seen by animals, they will be struck with terror. 6. After death, they will fall into the evil realms.

Regarding the thirty-five matters for the deprivation of a bhikṣu: once a bhikṣu has committed a grave offense and the formal act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) has been completed, he is deprived of these thirty-five matters and must not perform them.
First, he must not confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*). Second, he must not receive others as his dependents (*niśraya*).
Third, he must not maintain *śrāmaṇeras*. Fourth, he must not accept the community’s appointment to instruct bhikṣuṇīs.
1. One should not act as a teacher appointed by the Saṃgha. 2. One should not recite the Prātimokṣa. 3.
When the Saṃgha questions one on the meaning of the Vinaya, one should not answer. 4. One should not perform formal acts (*karmavācanā*) appointed by the Saṃgha. 5.

When the Saṃgha selects and gathers those of wisdom to deliberate on a matter together, one must not be included in the assembly. 6. One should not act as a messenger entrusted with a confidential mission appointed by the Saṃgha.
11. One must not enter a village too early. 12. One must not return at the close of day. 13.
One should associate with bhikṣus and should not associate with non-Buddhists. 14. One should be well-disposed toward following the instructions of the bhikṣus.
15. One should not speak contrary words. 16. The Saṃgha shall, according to the offense committed, perform a *kukkucca-kamma* (reproachful act) against one.
16. One should not commit [the offense] again. 17. One should also not commit a similar offense. 18.
One should also not commit an offense arising from that. 19. One should also not commit one more serious than this. 20.
One should not disparage the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) or the person performing the *karmavācanā*. 21. A virtuous bhikṣu should prepare seats and provide offerings.
20. One should accept [offerings]. 21. One should not accept having one's feet washed by another. 22.
One should not accept having foot-washing implements provided by another. 23. One should not accept having one's leather sandals brushed by another.
24. One should not accept having one's body rubbed by another. 25. One should not accept prostrations from another. 26. One should not accept...
28. He joins his palms [in salutation]. 29. He should not accept prostrations from others. 30. He should not accept being welcomed or escorted by others. 31.
He should not accept having his robes or bowl carried by others. 32. He should not initiate a formal act of *smṛti-vinaya* (reinstatement through recollection) against a bhikṣu.
33. He should not initiate a formal act of *pratijñā-kāraka* (admission of guilt) against a bhikṣu. 34. He should not... [text continues]
34. To testify to the matter of another bhikṣu; one should not obstruct the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā*. 35.
One should not engage in disputes with bhikṣus.
25. The deity who protects the precepts.
Not killing, bhikṣu, vīrya-dhāraṇī, śuddha-śuddhāni,
vairocana-prabhā-dharmanidhi-svara-hanini-bhava.
Not stealing: Dīpa, Ābhāsvara, Asura, Brahmā,
Puṇya, Brāhmaṇa, Bhūmida, Vitāna, Mahodaka, Yaśas.
No sexual misconduct; Buddha, Śāntarudra, Jayasūtra, Vajradhara, Arada, Rādha, Paranirvṛta.
Not speaking falsely: Atibrahmaḥ sañjñāyate,
tilaro tilaro, āgavandhara, dattabuddhimān,
matatātāre kṣamasmi te.
Not drinking liquor: Amalosa, Tuhuṇa, Nāmañjasa, Tuḍi, Sāvini, Ghaṇṭāpāṭhī,
Vindū, Viśālā, Kāmabhinna, Jaṅghānikā.

There are four types of Saṃghas: 1. A group of four monks: with the exception of the conferral of the full ordination (*upasampadā*), the invitation for self-reflection (*pravāraṇā*), and the absolution of offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*), other formal acts (*karmavācanā*) may be performed.
2. A group of five monks: with the exception of the conferral of the full ordination and the absolution of offenses, other formal acts may be performed.
3. A group of twenty monks: with the exception of the absolution of offenses, other formal acts may be performed. 4. A group of ten monks: all formal acts may be performed.

[The Procedure for] the Eight Difficulties: Whenever the Uposatha, the recitation of the precepts, the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), or other such rites are being performed, if one of the eight difficulties arises, an abbreviated recitation may be conducted.
The eight difficulties are: first, kings; second, bandits; third, water; fourth, fire; fifth, illness; sixth, humans; seventh, non-humans; eighth, fierce beasts.

If a bhikṣu commits any of the eight matters that constitute a "loss of the night" (rātriparihāṇi), he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. While practicing the *parivāsa* (probation), he must announce his status to the community every night.
If he fails to announce it regarding any of these eight matters, it is termed a "loss of the night. The eight matters are: first, going to another monastery without announcing;
second, having a visiting bhikṣu arrive without announcing; third, leaving the boundary for a legitimate reason without announcing; fourth, [moving] slowly within the monastery...
1. A bhikṣu who is traveling does not inform [the community]. 2. One who is ill does not send a messenger to inform [the community]. 3. Two or three people stay together in a single room.
4. One dwells in a place where no other bhikṣus reside. 5. One does not inform [the community] at the time of the half-monthly recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*.
If one violates even a single one of these matters, one loses the status for that night and incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
